title: MAINT: break a few circular imports

labels.name: maintenance
labels.description: Items related to regular maintenance tasks

body:
#### What does this implement/fix?

The imports in `scipy.spatial.transform` are order-sensitive: sorting them alphabetically gives:

    $ python -c 'import scipy.spatial.transform'
    ImportError: cannot import name 'Rotation' from partially initialized module 'scipy.spatial.transform' (most likely due to a circular import)

The same in some other modules. The PR fixes some latent bugs related to that, mostly by importing the sibling module instead of the parent module that re-exports things from the sibling module.

#### Additional information

Checked with uncycle (`pip install uncycle`) against the parent commit:

```
$ uncycle --baseline ../parent/scipy scipy 
scipy/_lib/_testutils.py:20: imports scipy
scipy/fftpack/_pseudo_diffs.py:14: imports scipy.fftpack
scipy/linalg/_expm_frechet.py:3: imports scipy.linalg
scipy/sparse/_sputils.py:9: imports scipy.sparse
scipy/stats/_continuous_distns.py:39: imports scipy.stats
scipy/stats/_correlation.py:3: imports scipy.stats
scipy/stats/_distribution_infrastructure.py:15: imports scipy.stats
scipy/stats/_fit.py:4: imports scipy.stats
scipy/stats/_morestats.py:11: imports scipy.stats
scipy/stats/_morestats.py:33: imports scipy.stats._wilcoxon
scipy/stats/_mstats_basic.py:47: imports scipy.stats._stats_py
scipy/stats/_mstats_basic.py:48: imports scipy.stats._stats_py
scipy/stats/_multivariate.py:19: imports scipy.stats._covariance
scipy/stats/_stats_py.py:67: imports scipy.stats
scipy/stats/contingency.py:34: imports scipy.stats
dependencies to remove decreased from 59 to 14
```

#### AI Generation Disclosure

Claude was used to run uncycle and fix some of the reported issues.

body:
#### Reference issue
Towards #25964 

#### What does this implement/fix?
Corrects return dtypes for several functions and adds some tests for all functions listed in the reference issue except for `fractional_matrix_power` since that one is quite tough to properly audit. Perhaps it is best to leave that for a follow-up since a quick attempt revealed that quite a lot of changes were needed and did not even cover all possible cases.

The added tests always at least check the shapes and dtypes of the return arguments. Where possible they also check whether the behavior is correct, but when the docs did not mention how exactly the return arguments should relate to the input this was not done. This applies for example to `clarkson_woodruff_transform` and `expm_frechet`.

#### Additional information
Some CI failures are expected:
- For `solve_toeplitz` it used to be the case that the arrays were always cast to either `float64` or `complex128`. This is now corrected to cast to `cdsz`, but does not explicitly guard against other exotic cases such as `float16`/`complex256` leading to some CI failures in `test_deprecations` since the cython code is not implemented to deal with this. Probably the best way to resolve this is to add the "normal" sequence of `_deprecate_dtypes -> _normalize_lapack_dtype` and probably adjust those tests accordingly?
- For `solve_discrete_lyapunov` I am getting some failures locally for `n=5` due to (excessively) large mismatches, but this seems to also be present on main so this might be something that warrants its own issue?

Furthermore, the testsuite for `solve_toeplitz` might now be excessively large.

title: ENH: add Wright's generalized Bessel function

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: A new feature or improvement

body:
#### Reference issue
This function is one crucial step towards #11291. See also mailing list thread https://mail.python.org/pipermail/scipy-dev/2020-January/023918.html.

#### What does this implement/fix?
This PR adds Wright's generalized Bessel function as `scipy.special.wright_bessel`, see https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.46.E1.

#### Additional information.
~~This is a pure Python implementation that aims for correctness and not for speed.~~ I did not find any public implementation as a reference.
As it is an entire function, the series representation is always valid. ~~I tried asymptotic expansions for large argument z, without any luck.~~

Edit:
So far, only non-negative values of rho=a, beta=b and z=x are implemented. There are 5 different approaches depending on the ranges of the arguments.

1. Taylor series expansion in x=0 [1], for x <= 1.
    Involves gamma funtions in each term.
2. Taylor series expansion in x=0 [2], for large a.
3. Taylor series in a=0, for tiny a and not too large x.
4. Asymptotic expansion for large x [3, 4].
    Suitable for large x while still small a and b.
5. Integral representation [5], in principle for all arguments.


References:
- [1] https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.46.E1
- [2] P. K. Dunn, G. K. Smyth (2005), Series evaluation of Tweedie exponential
     dispersion model densities. Statistics and Computing 15 (2005): 267-280.
- [3] E. M. Wright (1935), The asymptotic expansion of the generalized Bessel
     function. Proc. London Math. Soc. (2) 38, pp. 257-270.
     https://doi.org/10.1112/plms/s2-38.1.257
- [4] R. B. Paris (2017), The asymptotics of the generalised Bessel function,
     Mathematica Aeterna, Vol. 7, 2017, no. 4, 381 - 406,
     https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.03006
- [5] Y. F. Luchko (2008), Algorithms for Evaluation of the Wright Function for
     the Real Arguments' Values, Fractional Calculus and Applied Analysis 11(1)
     http://sci-gems.math.bas.bg/jspui/bitstream/10525/1298/1/fcaa-vol11-num1-2008-57p-75p.pdf

title: Fix bug when mixed dtype inputs are given to solve_discrete_lyapunov or solve_sylvester

title: BUG: maximum_bipartite_matching takes exponential time on layered graphs because the Hopcroft-Karp DFS never marks dead ends

labels.name: defect
labels.description: A clear bug or issue that prevents SciPy from being installed or used as expected

body:
### Describe your issue.

`scipy.sparse.csgraph.maximum_bipartite_matching`, and through it `structural_rank` and the feasibility check inside `min_weight_full_bipartite_matching`, take time exponential in the depth of a layered structure that ordinary sparse matrices contain. On the 94-vertex, 308-edge instance below the call takes 8.8 s, and the time doubles with every added level. On a real 15 231-by-15 231 Jacobian with 116 659 nonzeros from a finite-difference pipeline-network model (a chain-like pattern, available on request as `.npz`), the call does not return within 300 s, while a random pattern of the same size and density takes 0.16 s and a maximum-product matching of the same matrix in a Numba implementation takes 2 ms.

The cause is in `_hopcroft_karp` in `scipy/sparse/csgraph/_matching.pyx`. The depth-first phase pushes a level-(d+1) vertex `yu` onto the stack once for every level-d vertex `v` adjacent to it, and never marks a vertex whose subtree failed to reach a free column; only the vertices of a successful augmenting path get `dist[v] = INF`. A vertex reachable through k level-respecting paths is therefore expanded k times, and a subgraph in which every level has two vertices adjacent to both vertices of the next level is walked 2^depth times whenever no free column lies below it. The variable `could_augment` computed in that loop is never used, which suggests the pruning was intended. The textbook algorithm sets `dist[v] = INF` when the search from `v` fails, which bounds each phase by O(E) and gives the O(E sqrt V) total that the docstring promises. The code on `main` (checked 2026-09-10) is identical to 1.16.3 in this function.

### Reproducing Code Example

Columns `0..m` form a chain, columns `m+1..` a width-2 ladder of `L+1` blocks. The greedy first phase matches the chain and the ladder diagonally and leaves the last row `r` unmatched with the last chain column free. In the second phase the search from `r` pushes the chain entry first and the ladder entry last, so it explores the ladder first; the ladder has no free column below it, and every one of its ~2^(L+1) level-respecting paths is walked before the chain is tried. A perfect matching exists.

```python
import time
import numpy as np
import scipy.sparse as sps
from scipy.sparse.csgraph import maximum_bipartite_matching


def ladder_instance(L, m=None):
    m = L + 1 if m is None else m          # chain length >= ladder depth
    nA = 2 * L + 2
    A0 = m + 1                              # first ladder column
    rows, cols = [], []
    for k in range(m):                      # chain rows b_k: columns [B_k, B_k+1]
        rows += [k, k]; cols += [k, k + 1]
    for k in range(L + 1):                  # ladder block k: two rows, columns [A_2k .. A_2k+3]
        for r in (m + 2 * k, m + 2 * k + 1):
            for c in (2 * k, 2 * k + 1, 2 * k + 2, 2 * k + 3):
                if c < nA:
                    rows.append(r); cols.append(A0 + c)
    r = m + nA                              # root row, last in order: columns [B_0, A_0]
    rows += [r, r]; cols += [0, A0]
    n = m + nA + 1
    A = sps.csr_array((np.ones(len(rows)), (rows, cols)), shape=(n, n))
    A.sort_indices()
    return A


for L in (20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 30):
    A = ladder_instance(L)
    t = time.perf_counter()
    p = maximum_bipartite_matching(A, perm_type='column')
    print(f'L={L} n={A.shape[0]} nnz={A.nnz} unmatched={int((p < 0).sum())} time={time.perf_counter() - t:.3f} s')
```

### Error message

No error; the observed times.

```
L=20 n=64 nnz=208 unmatched=0 time=0.008 s
L=22 n=70 nnz=228 unmatched=0 time=0.033 s
L=24 n=76 nnz=248 unmatched=0 time=0.133 s
L=26 n=82 nnz=268 unmatched=0 time=0.560 s
L=28 n=88 nnz=288 unmatched=0 time=2.187 s
L=30 n=94 nnz=308 unmatched=0 time=8.780 s
```

`structural_rank(A)` and `min_weight_full_bipartite_matching(A)` on the same instance take the same time, since both call `_hopcroft_karp`.

### Suggested fix

Explore every left vertex at most once per phase, in the DFS loop of `_hopcroft_karp`:

```cython
                    stack_head -= 1
                    v = stack[stack_head]
                    if dist[v] == INF:       # already explored in this phase
                        continue
                    dist_v = dist[v]
                    dist[v] = INF            # a failed search from v must not be repeated
                    for up in range(indptr[v], indptr[v + 1]):
                        u = indices[up]
                        yu = y[u]
                        if dist[yu] == dist_v + 1:
                            ...
```

Verified with a line-by-line Python port of `_hopcroft_karp`: on the L = 20 instance the stack pops fall from 2 097 238 to 128; the port with the fix returns the same matching cardinality as scipy on the ladder instances with L = 12, 16 and 20 and on random 500- and 3000-vertex graphs; on the 15 231-by-15 231 matrix it finds a perfect matching in 10 phases and 23 453 pops, where the unmodified port is still in phase 8 after 20 million pops. The stack never held more than n + 1 entries in any of these runs, so the fixed-size stack is not involved.

### SciPy/NumPy/Python version and system information

scipy 1.16.3, numpy 2.3.5, Python 3.11.13, macOS 26.6 on arm64 (Apple M4).

#### What does this implement/fix?
<!-- Write this part yourself. Facts to cover, then delete these notes:
- Cause: in the depth-first phase of `_hopcroft_karp`, a vertex whose search fails is never marked. A vertex reachable along k level-respecting paths is explored k times, so the time grows exponentially with the depth of the layered graph.
- Fix: mark `v` with `dist[v] = INF` when it is popped. Each vertex is explored at most once per phase, which gives O(E) per phase and the documented O(E sqrt(V)) total.
- A popped vertex that is already marked is skipped. This happens only when the input has duplicate entries. Duplicate entries can also overflow the fixed-size stack; that bug is older than this PR and will be reported separately (add the issue number once filed).
- Removed: the unused `could_augment`, and the `dist[v] = INF` in the unwind loop, since every vertex on the path is already marked when popped.
- Not chosen: marking at push also marks siblings that were pushed but never explored, so a phase can miss vertex-disjoint shortest augmenting paths and the O(E sqrt(V)) bound no longer holds.
- New test `test_maximum_bipartite_matching_dead_end_explored_once`: a free row whose search must fail walks the whole ladder in any visiting order. It uses `@pytest.mark.timeout(2)`, as `sparse/tests/test_csr.py` does. On `main` it fails with `Timeout (>2.0s)`, and the run takes 9.6 s. With the fix, all of `test_matching.py` runs in 0.78 s.

title: MAINT: linalg: improve input shape consistency checks

labels.name: Documentation
labels.description: Issues related to the SciPy documentation. Also check https://github.com/scipy/scipy.org

labels.name: maintenance
labels.description: Items related to regular maintenance tasks

body:
#### Reference issue
https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/24148#issuecomment-5284580100

#### What does this implement/fix?
Previously, the `_apply_over_batch` would only validate input shapes if an input had zero size.
This changes it to perform the input validation on all input.

For instance, `solve_sylvester(np.eye(2), np.eye(3), np.eye(2))` raises the following in `main`:

```
ValueError: shapes (2,2) and (3,3) not aligned:
2 (dim 1) != 3 (dim 0)
```

With this PR:
```
ValueError: The core shape(s) of the array argument(s):
a: (2, 2), b: (3, 3), q: (2, 2)
is/are incompatible with the shapes in the signature:
a: (i, i), b: (j, j), q: (i, j)
```
Of course, we could add additional logic to make the error as specific as we like.

Even if functions had readable error messages to begin with, this makes the messages consistent so users only have to learn to interpret one type of message. As an added benefit, we could now delete a ton of of function-specific input validation code.

The PR also explains NEP 5 signatures in the `linalg` batch tutorial and fixes some bugs.

#### Additional information 
If we don't want to turn this on for all functions, we can add an option to `_apply_over_batch` to opt in to the input validation. In any case, there's a lot of other little improvements in this PR.

#### AI Generation Disclosure
I used Codex to audit the messages produced for incompatible shapes in `main` and this PR (in its various stages). It founds some bugs; I fixed them.

title: BUG: cluster.hierarchy.fcluster: reject t < 1 for maxclust criteria

labels.name: defect
labels.description: A clear bug or issue that prevents SciPy from being installed or used as expected

body:
#### Reference issue

Closes gh-21206.

#### What does this implement/fix?

`fcluster` with `criterion="maxclust"` and `t=0` gives a different answer depending on what
is in memory , instead of complaining .

`cluster_maxclust_monocrit` ends with `MC[upper_idx]` , but `MC` only holds `n-1` values ,
so the last legal index is `n-2` . `upper_idx` starts at `n-1` and only comes down when a
threshold gives few enough clusters . testing `i = n-2` always puts the whole tree into one
cluster , so that test only fails when `max_nc < 1` . in that one case `upper_idx` is never
lowered and `MC[n-1]` is read one past the end of the array .

`_hierarchy.pyx` is compiled with `boundscheck=False` , so nothing catches it and the cutoff
is whatever happens to sit in that memory . with `t=0` on six points the result is six
singleton clusters . passing an `MC` one slot longer with a known value in slot `n-1` changes
the answer , which is what showed where it was reading from .

no `t` can ever produce fewer than one cluster , so the input is rejected instead . that
removes the only path that reaches the read rather than hiding it . `t >= 1` is unchanged ,
and `distance` and `inconsistent` still take `t=0` .

#### Additional information

`t=0.5` is rejected too , it truncated to zero and reached the same line . `t=1.5` still
works .

six new cases cover `maxclust` and `maxclust_monocrit` for `t` of 0 , -1 and 0.5 . they fail
on main with "DID NOT RAISE ValueError" . `pytest scipy/cluster/` gives 225 passed , 6
skipped .

#### AI Generation Disclosure

i used claude code ( claude opus 5 ) to help look into the cause and to draft the patch and
the test . i went over the change myself , confirmed the out of bounds read , and ran the
tests locally .

body: ### Issue with current documentation: The documentation of `scipy` states that ([doc](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/tutorial/linalg.html)): > `scipy.linalg` contains **all** the functions in `numpy.linalg.` plus some other more advanced ones not contained in `numpy.linalg`. However, several (commonly used) functionalities from `numpy.linalg` are, unfortunately, not available in `scipy.linalg`, including (but not limited to) `numpy.linalg.matrix_rank(...)` and `numpy.linalg.matrix_power(...)`, which are used abundantly. This is misleading to users, who would expect the above to be available based on the mentioned documentation, tempting them to rely solely on `scipy.linalg` (which, as of now, is unfortunately not possible). ### Idea or request for content: I myself see two solutions: 1. Update the documentation to make it explicit that `scipy.linalg` cannot be used as a one-on-one replacement for `numpy.linalg`, as not all functionalities are provided equally. 2. (Preferred) Add the functionalities provided by `numpy.linalg` to `scipy.linalg`. I do not know how hard it is to implement/wrap all of the provided `numpy.linalg` functionality, but it would be amazing in streamlining code to be able to rely solely on `import scipy.linalg as la` instead of having to (arbitrarily) switch from SciPy to NumPy. ### Additional context (e.g. screenshots, GIFs)

title: BUG: sparse.csgraph: handle duplicate CSR entries in bipartite matching

labels.name: defect
labels.description: A clear bug or issue that prevents SciPy from being installed or used as expected

labels.name: needs-decision
labels.description: Items that need further discussion before they are merged or closed

labels.name: Cython
labels.description: Issues with the internal Cython code base

body:
#### Reference issue

Closes gh-26160

#### What does this implement/fix?

`maximum_bipartite_matching`, `structural_rank` and
`min_weight_full_bipartite_matching` crash (or hang, or return garbage) when the CSR input stores the same entry more than once. `_hopcroft_karp` in `scipy/sparse/csgraph/_matching.pyx` pushes `y[u]` onto a fixed-size DFS stack once for every stored entry that passes the level check, so a row stored `K` times pushes the same row `K` times. The stack has only `i + 1` slots and the extension is compiled with `boundscheck(False)`, so the extra pushes overwrite heap memory.

CSR arrays may legitimately contain duplicate entries — `tocsr()` does not always merge them, and `eliminate_zeros()` / `.T.tocsr()` keep them. A `coo` input is not affected because converting to CSR merges duplicates.

**Changes**

- `scipy/sparse/csgraph/_matching.pyx`:
  - `maximum_bipartite_matching`: merge duplicate entries (copy + `sum_duplicates`) when the input has no canonical format, before calling `_hopcroft_karp`.
  - `min_weight_full_bipartite_matching`: same normalization, before the feasibility search and `_lapjvsp`. Duplicate weights are summed, matching scipy's standard semantics for duplicates.
- `structural_rank` (in `_reordering.pyx`) delegates to `maximum_bipartite_matching`, so it is covered automatically.
- Tests added in `scipy/sparse/csgraph/tests/test_matching.py` for all three functions using `K = 100_000` duplicate entries, which overflow the stack on every platform before this fix.

**Why this approach**

Canonicalizing the input keeps the documented space complexity of `_hopcroft_karp` ($O(|E| \sqrt{|V|})$ time, linear in the number of rows) and also protects `_lapjvsp` (which reads the same arrays in `min_weight_full_bipartite_matching`); growing the stack to `nnz + 1` would break the space guarantee and leave `_lapjvsp` exposed.

#### Verification

- Pre-fix behavior of the issue's reproducer on SciPy 1.18.1 (Python 3.14, Linux):
  - `maximum_bipartite_matching`: **segmentation fault** (exit 139)
  - `structural_rank`: **hang** (no completion within 20 s)
  - `min_weight_full_bipartite_matching`: **segmentation fault** (exit 139)
- Post-fix: same input is normalized to a canonical 3-entry CSR, and the searches return the correct maximum matching (both partitions), structural rank 2, and a valid full matching M-bM-^@M-^T verified on the compiled extension by canonicalizing before the search, mirroring exactly what the added two-line wrappers do.
- The edited `_matching.pyx` passes a full Cython compile.
- Full from-source build (meson + OpenBLAS, Cython 3.3.0) of the branch: `test_matching.py` 37 passed; `scipy/sparse/csgraph/tests/` 1350 passed, 58 skipped; CSR/CSC ABI smoke 37 passed, 1 skipped.

#### Additional information

The pre-fix and patched `_matching.pyx` variants were each compiled with Cython and hot-swapped in place, so the crash signatures above come from the real compiled extension rather than an emulation. Review responses are in the thread above.

#### AI Generation Disclosure

AI assistance was used in the preparation of this pull request.

- **Tool:** the `big-pickle` model (model ID `opencode/big-pickle`), used through the `opencode` command-line coding agent.
- **How it was used:** to analyse the stack overflow in `_hopcroft_karp` and identify the duplicate-entry push pattern, to implement the normalization guards in `scipy/sparse/csgraph/_matching.pyx`, to write the regression tests in `scipy/sparse/csgraph/tests/test_matching.py`, and to produce the before/after verification (including compiling and hot-swapping pre-fix and patched `_matching.pyx` variants to obtain the real crash signatures).
- **What is AI-generated:** the `_matching.pyx` changes, the added tests, and the wording of this description.
- **Author review:** I reviewed and understand every change, reproduced the original crash and hang locally, and can explain the reasoning and the review responses above. Per SciPy's policy I take full responsibility for this contribution.

title: QUERY: stats.ansari should use a different null mean and variance for the tie-corrected asymptotic p-value when ties cross the middle rank

labels.name: query
labels.description: A question or suggestion that requires further information

body:
*Note: see https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/26264#issuecomment-5827315975; this issue is about the asymptotic null distribution in the presence of ties, not disagreement between the asymptotic and theoretically exact test results.*

### Describe your issue.

`stats.ansari([1, 2, 3], [3, 4, 5])` returns p = 0.778, but the correct answer is p = 1.0.

**Why 1.0:** the observed statistic is 6.5, which equals its mean under the null hypothesis, so z = 0 and p = 1. scipy's own exact permutation method — `stats.ansari(x, y, method=stats.PermutationMethod())` — also returns p = 1.0. So two methods of the same function disagree.

**Cause** (`scipy/stats/_morestats.py`): the Ansari test scores each observation and uses the sum of the first sample's scores as the statistic. With ties, scipy assigns average ranks (≈ line 3164, `symrank = min(midrank, N+1-midrank)`). When a tie straddles the middle rank, the total sum of all scores changes: in my example the sum is 13, whereas without ties it would be 12. But the mean formula (≈ line 3202, `mnAB = n(N+2)/4`) and the tie-corrected variance formula (≈ lines 3206–3210) both assume this sum is constant, so both the mean and the variance are wrong.

**Correct formulas:** this is the standard result for linear rank statistics; see Lehmann, *Nonparametrics* (1975), Appendix, or Hájek–Šidák–Sen, *Theory of Rank Tests*.

* mean = n × mean of all scores
* variance = m·n / (N(N−1)) × Σ(scoreᵢ − mean score)²

where n and m are the sample sizes and N = n + m.

**Suggested fix:** with ties, compute the mean and variance from the actual scores using the formulas above. If a tie does not cross the middle rank, the result is identical to the current behavior, so other cases are unaffected.

**Additional notes:** R's `ansari.test` uses the same formulas as scipy, so it cannot be used as a reference; the exact permutation test is used here instead. A larger example: x=[1,2,2,3,4], y=[2,3,3,5,6,6]. scipy gives 0.860, and the exact permutation test gives 0.944. So the problem is not limited to tiny samples.

**AI usage disclosure:** I used an AI assistant to help identify this problem and write the reproduction script. The description above is my own, and the reproduction was run on my own computer.

### Reproducing Code Example

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
import scipy

print("scipy", scipy.__version__)

# ties cross the middle rank: the observed statistic equals its null mean,
# so the asymptotic p-value should be 1.0
x = [1, 2, 3]
y = [3, 4, 5]
res = stats.ansari(x, y)
print(f"ansari(x, y): statistic = {res.statistic}, pvalue = {res.pvalue}")
res_exact = stats.ansari(x, y, method=stats.PermutationMethod())
print(f"ansari(..., PermutationMethod): statistic = {res_exact.statistic}, pvalue = {res_exact.pvalue}")

# larger example
x2 = [1, 2, 2, 3, 4]
y2 = [2, 3, 3, 5, 6, 6]
res2 = stats.ansari(x2, y2)
print(f"larger ansari: pvalue = {res2.pvalue}")
res2_exact = stats.ansari(x2, y2, method=stats.PermutationMethod())
print(f"larger PermutationMethod: pvalue = {res2_exact.pvalue}")
```

### Error message

```shell
No error is raised; the p-value itself is wrong. Output:

scipy 1.18.1
ansari(x, y): statistic = 6.5, pvalue = 0.7781596861761658
ansari(..., PermutationMethod): statistic = 6.5, pvalue = 1.0
larger ansari: pvalue = 0.8599267005242307
larger PermutationMethod: pvalue = 0.9437229437229437
```

```shell
1.18.1 2.5.3 3.14.7 (main, Aug  5 2026, 10:29:49) [Clang 21.0.0 (clang-2100.1.1.101)]
macOS 26.6.2 arm64
```

### Describe your issue.

When HiGHS methods are used, `linprog` accepts a `primal_feasibility_tolerance` option.
When HiGHS returns, ``_check_result`` in ``_linprog_util.py`` re-checks the solution against a fixed threshold of `np.sqrt(tol) * 10` with `tol=1e-9`, i.e. about 3.16e-4.
`tol` is not even a supported option for HiGHS, it's for the older methods.

So if `primal_feasibility_tolerance` is set higher, HiGHS can give a correct solution which ``_check_result`` then rejects with `status=4, success=False`.

I see gh-11326 had a similar issue. It was closed by gh-15512, which made HiGHS the default and deprecated the older methods. But ``_check_result`` still runs for HiGHS results.
The default tolerances don't cause any issues.

The included code snippet isolates the issue with one solution over and one below this arbitrary tolerance from `tol` (≈ 3.16e-4), and shows correct solution from HiGHS being accepted or rejected depending only on this tolerance, even though both are within the `primal_feasibility_tolerance=1e-3` I set.

I found this issue while working on issue gh-18789.

### Reproducing Code Example

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import linprog

# minimize x  subject to  x >= v  (written as a row: -x <= -v),  x >= 0
# With presolve off, HiGHS starts at x = 0, which violates the row by v.
# If v < primal_feasibility_tolerance, HiGHS correctly accepts x = 0.
for v in [2e-4, 5e-4]:
    res = linprog([1.0], A_ub=[[-1.0]], b_ub=[-v], bounds=[(0, None)],
                  method="highs",
                  options={"presolve": False,
                           "primal_feasibility_tolerance": 1e-3})
    print(f"v={v:g}: x={res.x}, slack={res.slack}, "
          f"status={res.status}, success={res.success}")
    if not res.success:
        print(res.message)

# linprog's post-solve check threshold (_linprog_util.py, _check_result):
print("threshold:", np.sqrt(1e-9) * 10)
```

### Error message

```shell
v=0.0002: x=[0.], slack=[-0.0002], status=0, success=True
v=0.0005: x=[0.], slack=[-0.0005], status=4, success=False
The solution does not satisfy the constraints within the required tolerance of 3.16E-04, yet no errors were raised and there is no certificate of infeasibility or unboundedness. Check whether the slack and constraint residuals are acceptable; if not, consider enabling presolve, adjusting the tolerance option(s), and/or using a different method. Please consider submitting a bug report.
threshold: 0.00031622776601683794
```

title: DOC: interpolate: document triangulation ambiguity in griddata

labels.name: Documentation
labels.description: Issues related to the SciPy documentation. Also check https://github.com/scipy/scipy.org

body:
#### Reference issue
Closes gh-23990

#### What does this implement/fix?
The `griddata` documentation did not mention that interpolation results can differ between machines, even with the same input data. I added a note to the docstring explaining that `griddata` uses Delaunay triangulation for the `linear` and `cubic` methods. On a rectilinear grid, the triangulation is not unique because the four corners of a rectangle are co-circular. The diagonal selected can therefore vary due to floating-point rounding across platforms or Qhull versions, which can lead to slightly different interpolated values. For data on a regular grid, the documentation now points users to `RegularGridInterpolator` (or `interpn`) to avoid this triangulation ambiguity.

title: ENH: explicit fit for generalized Pareto distribution (genpareto)

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: A new feature or improvement

body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

I come across this when browsing through general methods for fitting the location parameter of a distribution. SciPy already contains explicit `fit` methods for `pareto` (gh-12545) and `powerlaw` (gh-13053) distributions. It would be nice to “complete the puzzle” by implementing `fit` for the `genpareto` distribution. This would also tick a box in gh-17832.

### Describe the solution you'd like.

This can be broken down into a few steps:

1. Improve the documentation regarding the relation between `genpareto`, `pareto`, and `powerlaw`. The three actually share the same density function, but with different domain of the shape parameter. As a result, once the fit method of the latter two are implemented, the first one is ready almost “for free”.

2. Decide what to do when the _global_ maximum of the likelihood function is unbounded. At the moment this is handled differently between `pareto` and `powerlaw`: in the former, a _local_ maximum is sought and returned; in the latter, some artificial value “just” within bound is returned. Literature appears to suggest to use local MLE when it exists, and to conclude that MLE is not appropriate when no local maximum exists and the global maximum is unbounded. I prefer this approach as it is more prudent than returning some spurious value “just” within bound.

3. Review the fit method of `pareto` and `powerlaw`. 
- When location or scale is known, explicit formulas are used and there’s nothing more to do. 
- When location and/or scale is unknown but shape is known, a small improvement could be made to the current implementation to bound the root of the first derivative of the log likelihood function by explicit formulas rather than trial and error.
- When location, shape and scale are all unknown, a method is described in [Grimshaw (1993)](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00401706.1993.10485040). It’s essentially the same as what `pareto.fit` does (local MLE), but with more elaborate discussion on the property of the likelihood function and its roots (existence and multiplicity). I need to look more closely to see whether the current method is adequate in the (not so corner) corner cases.

4. Implement `genpareto.fit` reusing the code of `pareto.fit` and `powerlaw.fit`.

### Describe alternatives you've considered.

title: TST: linalg: fix Pyodide hang and crash in wrapper GC tests

labels.name: maintenance
labels.description: Items related to regular maintenance tasks

labels.name: CI
labels.description: Items related to the CI tools such as CircleCI, GitHub Actions or Azure

body:
#### Reference issue
Closes gh-26266.

#### What does this implement/fix?
Test-only changes in `scipy/linalg/tests/` that stop the Pyodide job from hanging and crashing:

1. **Skip `test_wrapper_module_collected` on WASM** (`test_lapack.py`). This test loads a second, fresh copy of the `_fblas`/`_flapack` extension module. On Pyodide it sometimes hangs until the 45-minute job timeout cancels the run. The last 4 cancelled Emscripten/Pyodide runs all stopped at this test (details in gh-26266). This follows the approach agreed in gh-25713: skip the test so CI stops hanging, and look into the root cause separately.

2. **Use `gc.get_referents` in `test_wrapper_traverses_its_type`** (`test_lapack.py` and `test_blas.py`). With the first test skipped, the [next Pyodide run](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/actions/runs/36097918127/job/107954087650?pr=26267) got further and then crashed on this test with a fatal `RuntimeError: null function or function signature mismatch`. The test used `gc.get_referrers(type(func))`, which calls `tp_traverse` on *every* GC-tracked object in the interpreter. WASM checks function-pointer signatures strictly, so an unrelated extension type loaded earlier in that pytest-split group took the whole process down. The wrapper's own `tp_traverse` signature is correct. The test now checks that `type(func)` is in `gc.get_referents(func)`, which calls only the wrapper's traverse. That is the property under test, and it still fails if the wrapper stops reporting its type. This test keeps running on WASM. `test_blas.py` had the same pattern and got the same change.

3. **Skip `test_self_referential_sequence_raises_recursion_error` on WASM** (`test_blas_lapack_wrappers.py`, added in gh-26243). After the rebase, the [Pyodide run](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/actions/runs/36124404096/job/108037222803) crashed on this test with a fatal `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`. The test passes a self-referential list as a scalar argument and expects `RecursionError`. On Pyodide the WASM stack runs out before the interpreter's recursion limit is reached, and that is fatal for the whole pytest-split group. The test still runs on all other platforms.

#### Additional information
The hang in (1) is intermittent, so a single green Pyodide run on this PR doesn't prove that fix. `test_wrapper_module_collected` still runs on all other platforms.

labels.name: CI

body:
The `Emscripten/Pyodide` workflow intermittently hangs until the 45-minute `timeout-minutes` cancels the job. No test fails. The hang always happens at the same point: in test group 3, right after the last test in `linalg/tests/test_interpolative.py`.

### Where it hangs

Last line printed before the cancellation ([run 36089927326](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/actions/runs/36089927326/job/107930027185)):

```
03:34:04 linalg/tests/test_interpolative.py::TestInterpolativeDecomposition::test_svd_aslinearoperator_shape_check PASSED [ 55%]
04:05:25 ##[error]The operation was canceled.
```

In a green run (48243f6e46), the next tests are:

```
01:03:47 linalg/tests/test_interpolative.py::...::test_svd_aslinearoperator_shape_check PASSED [ 55%]
01:03:48 linalg/tests/test_lapack.py::test_wrapper_module_collected[_fblas-daxpy] PASSED [ 55%]
01:03:48 linalg/tests/test_lapack.py::test_wrapper_module_collected[_fblas_64-daxpy] SKIPPED [ 55%]
01:03:49 linalg/tests/test_lapack.py::test_wrapper_module_collected[_flapack-dgesv] PASSED [ 55%]
```

So the test that hangs is `test_wrapper_module_collected` in `scipy/linalg/tests/test_lapack.py`.

### It's recurring

These cancelled runs all stop at that same line:

| commit | last test output | cancelled |
|---|---|---|
| c542b65171 | 03:34:04 | 04:05:25 |
| a5283b62f2 | 23:55:59 | 00:27:00 |
| dd556733e7 | 23:34:57 | 00:05:41 |
| 70eea68782 | 20:47:24 | 21:14:33 |

Green runs in between pass the same test in about 1 s, so the hang is intermittent. The commits that triggered these runs don't touch the code involved.

### Likely cause

`test_wrapper_module_collected` was added in 7fda41d859 (BUG: linalg: Remove duplicate wrapper heap-type references). It uses `spec_from_file_location` + `exec_module` to load a second, fresh copy of the `_fblas` / `_flapack` extension module, then checks that `gc.collect()` frees it. Loading the same large shared library a second time under Emscripten is the probable source of the hang. This has not been reproduced locally on Pyodide.

This looks unrelated to the libffi / heap-size hang in #25713, which pytest-split works around.

### Proposed fix

As agreed in #25713, skip it on WASM so CI stops hanging, and investigate separately:

```python
from scipy._lib._testutils import IS_WASM

@pytest.mark.skipif(IS_WASM, reason="re-loading extension modules hangs in WASM")
@pytest.mark.parametrize('module_name, routine', [...])
def test_wrapper_module_collected(module_name, routine):
```

ENH: optimize.bisect: improve worst case performance

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: A new feature or improvement

body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

I come across an interesting point regarding the bisection root finder when browsing @SimpleArt‘s (MIT licensed) project https://github.com/SimpleArt/pyroot. The standard bisection method starts with an initial bracket $[a_0,b_0]$ and repeatedly evaluates the function on $x_{k+1}:=(a_k+b_k)/2$ and shrinks the bracket according to the sign of $f(x_{k+1})$ in the obvious manner.

The author [points out](https://github.com/SimpleArt/pyroot/wiki/Binary-Search) that, when bisecting an independent variable $x$ stored in `float64` format, it is more efficient to bisect the _bit pattern_ of $x$ rather than the _value_ of $x$. For example, given the bracket  $[1,10^{100}]$, rather than checking (roughly) $5\times 10^{99}$, check (roughly) $10^{50}$ instead.

Since $x$ has 64 bits, this strategy ensures 1 ULP precision is attained with no more than 65 function evaluations. This worst case performance is significantly better than the standard bisection method, which would require 1000+ function evaluations in the worst case to achieve 1 ULP accuracy.



### Describe the solution you'd like.

Enrich the `bisect` method with an option to bisect the set of floating point numbers within the initial bracket.

title: BUG: stats.mannwhitneyu: reduce float32 error in the U statistic

labels.name: defect
labels.description: A clear bug or issue that prevents SciPy from being installed or used as expected

body:
#### Reference issue
Closes gh-24777.

#### What does this implement/fix?
Following up on the discussion in gh-24777: rather than upcasting, compute the statistic more
favourably at the same precision.

`U1` was formed as `R1 - n1*(n1+1)/2`. `R1` is much larger than `U1`, so in float32 it is
accumulated where the representable values are further apart, and the subtraction carries
that coarseness into the result. In the example from the issue, `R1` is about 2.4e7, where
float32 spacing is 2.0, while `U1` is about 6.1e6, where it is 0.5.

This subtracts `(n1 + 1)/2` from each rank before summing, which is algebraically the same
but keeps the accumulation at the magnitude of `U1`. For the example in the issue, the float32
statistic is now `6091893.5`, matching float64, instead of `6091892.0`. The result dtype is
unchanged.

`n1` comes from `_count_nonmasked`, so it is a Python `int` for regular arrays and a per-slice
`MArray` for masked input, where slices can have different counts. The offset is built with
`xp.asarray(..., dtype=ranks.dtype)` so both cases work without promoting the ranks, and it
is broadcast against the last axis. The existing `test_marray.py::test_mannwhitneyu` already
masks elements so that slices have different counts, and it still passes.

#### Additional information
Limitation: this removes the error from accumulating and then cancelling. It can't help when
`U` itself is too large for float32 to represent closely; for example with `n1 = n2 = 50000`
the statistic is around 1.25e9, where float32 spacing is 128.

Tests run locally with `SCIPY_ARRAY_API=1`: `test_hypotests.py`, `test_marray.py`,
`test_stats.py`, `test_axis_nan_policy.py`, all passing. The new test fails on `main` and
passes with this change.

`claude-opus-5-5` (medium effort) for the implementation. It wrote the code change, the new
test, and this description, and ran the tests listed above. I reviewed the change before

body:
### Describe your issue.

Hello,

From v1.17.0, `scipy.stats.mannwhitney` can be unstable and return (measurable) different results whether the input is `float32` or `float64`, even if composed of round numbers only.

I believe this is due to [this line](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/8c75ae75176236f233824e9a0483c26a69e6dfec/scipy/stats/_mannwhitneyu.py#L449) where the ranks are cast to the input's dtype, which was introduced in v1.17.0 through [23870](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/23870/changes#top). If input is `float32` and contains enough elements, ranksums (hence u-statistic) differ. 
Because not an overflow (but more a floating point rounding error) no warning is issued (which is the case if input is `float16`. Overflow warning is issued at `U2 = n1 * n2 - U1`).

MRE below (note that p-values do differ, consequently).

`_rankdata` returns ranks as `float64`. Removing this `xp.astype` would restore a stable behavior, but I don't know the rationale behind casting ranks to the input's dtype.

### Reproducing Code Example

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import mannwhitneyu
import scipy
print(f"Scipy version: {scipy.__version__}") # => Scipy version: 1.17.0

rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
x = rng.poisson(1, size=(6000, ))  # Those are integers
y = rng.poisson(1, size=(2000, ))  # Those are integers 
np.testing.assert_allclose(x.astype(np.float32), x.astype(np.float64), atol=0, rtol=0)  # passes, because round numbers
np.testing.assert_allclose(y.astype(np.float32), y.astype(np.float64), atol=0, rtol=0)  # passes, because round numbers

res_f32 = mannwhitneyu(x.astype(np.float32), y.astype(np.float32), alternative="two-sided", method="asymptotic", use_continuity=True)
res_f64 = mannwhitneyu(x.astype(np.float64), y.astype(np.float64), alternative="two-sided", method="asymptotic", use_continuity=True)
print(f"{res_f32.statistic}") # => 6091892.0
print(f"{res_f64.statistic}") # => 6091893.5
```

#### AI Generation Disclosure
No AI yet except that I had GPT-5.6 Sol analyze a log of all the `shapes`, `x_shape`, and `y_shape` generated by `draw_distribution_from_family` (main vs PR) to check that we're still getting good coverage. Turns out we're getting better coverage just with randomness, and parametrizing over `shape_options` gives us more control to add specific cases.

<details>

# Shape and broadcasting coverage: `main.npz` versus `PR2.npz`

## Executive summary

`PR2.npz` is much more effective at generating distinct, nontrivial broadcasting configurations within ranks 0 through 3. Despite containing five fewer records, it has 1,543 distinct exact configurations, compared with 888 in `main.npz`. It also uses scalars less often and makes two or more operands broadcast in 93.2% of records, compared with 74.4% in `main.npz`.

`main.npz` has one important advantage: it covers higher dimensionality. Its results reach rank 6, whereas every result in `PR2.npz` has rank at most 3. Consequently, `main.npz` has a larger raw vocabulary of shapes, but much of that advantage comes from ranks 4 through 6 rather than denser coverage at ordinary ranks.

The strongest combined strategy would use PR2-style generation for ranks 0 through 3 and retain a small, deliberate set of rank-4 through rank-6 cases.

## Data and methodology

Each record was normalized to

```text
(tuple(parameter_shapes), x_shape, y_shape)
```

NumPy integer dimensions were converted to Python integers before comparisons. All parameter shapes, the `x` shape, and the `y` shape were treated as separate broadcasting operands. The broadcast-result shape was computed with `numpy.broadcast_shapes`.

The archives contain only shape information. They do not identify the distribution or operation associated with each record. Therefore, two records with the same shapes may still test different implementations. Counts of duplicates in this report measure duplication of shape configurations, not necessarily redundant tests.

## Definitions

The short labels used below have the following precise meanings.

**Exact configuration**

The complete ordered combination of all parameter shapes, the `x` shape, and the `y` shape. Parameter order is significant. Two records are exact duplicates only when all these shapes agree.

**Structural broadcast pattern**

A configuration after discarding the particular values of ordinary dimensions while retaining:

- the number of parameter operands;
- every operand's rank;
- operand order;
- on every aligned axis, whether each operand has a missing leading axis, dimension zero, dimension one, or an ordinary dimension greater than one.

Thus, structurally equivalent examples such as `(2, 1)` with `(1, 3)` and `(4, 1)` with `(1, 2)` count as the same pattern. Zero is kept distinct because zero-length broadcasting has special behavior.

**Implicit leading-axis expansion** or **rank padding**

At least one operand has fewer axes than the broadcast result. NumPy aligns shapes from the right, which is equivalent to prepending dimensions of size one to the shorter operand. A scalar broadcasting to any nonscalar result is included in this category.

**Mixed operand ranks**

Not all operands have the same rank. For these mutually broadcastable records, this is equivalent to saying that at least one operand undergoes implicit leading-axis expansion.

**Singleton expansion**

At least one explicit input dimension of size one aligns with a result dimension that is not one. This includes both ordinary cases such as `1 -> 4` and zero-length cases such as `1 -> 0`. Merely prepending an implicit dimension to a shorter operand does not by itself count as singleton expansion.

**No broadcasting required**

Every operand shape is already exactly equal to the result shape. This is stricter than merely saying that the shapes are mutually broadcastable. For example, `()` with `(3,)` does require broadcasting under this definition.

**Operand changed to the result shape**

An operand's original shape is not exactly equal to the broadcast-result shape. This includes changes caused by rank padding, singleton expansion, or both. It describes logical shape expansion; it does not imply that NumPy materializes a copied array.

**Zero-length dimension present**

At least one operand has an explicit dimension of size zero. Because every record is mutually broadcastable, the corresponding result axis is also zero-length.

**Zero against singleton**

On at least one aligned axis, one operand has an explicit zero and another has an explicit one. Missing leading axes do not count as explicit singleton dimensions for this metric. For example, `(0, 3)` with `(1, 3)` qualifies and broadcasts to `(0, 3)`.

**Same-rank, multidirectional singleton expansion**

At least two nonscalar operands have the same rank as the result and expand explicit singleton dimensions on different axes. For example, `(3, 1)` with `(1, 4)` broadcasts to `(3, 4)`: the first operand expands on the second axis and the second operand expands on the first.

**Three operands owning different result axes**

At least three distinct operands uniquely provide ordinary dimensions greater than one on three distinct result axes. On each such axis, the other operands have either a singleton dimension or a missing leading axis. A canonical example is `(2, 1, 1)`, `(1, 3, 1)`, and `(1, 1, 4)`, which broadcast to `(2, 3, 4)`.

**All operands scalar**

Every parameter shape, the `x` shape, and the `y` shape is `()`.

## Overall diversity

| Metric | `main.npz` | `PR2.npz` |
|---|---:|---:|
| Records | 2,025 | 2,020 |
| Distinct exact configurations | 888 (43.9%) | 1,543 (76.4%) |
| Repeated records by exact shape | 1,137 | 477 |
| Largest multiplicity of one exact configuration | 232 | 49 |
| Distinct structural broadcast patterns | 877 | 1,223 |
| Distinct input shapes across all roles | 269 | 155 |
| Distinct broadcast-result shapes | 273 | 156 |

PR2 produces 655 more distinct exact configurations with five fewer records. Its lower raw count of distinct shapes is explained by its rank cap: PR2 draws from a compact rank-0-through-rank-3 universe, while main reaches rank 6.

The most common exact configuration in both archives is the one-parameter all-scalar case:

```text
parameter shapes = [()], x = (), y = () -> result = ()
```

It occurs 232 times in main and 49 times in PR2.

## Rank coverage

### Broadcast-result ranks

| Result rank | `main.npz` | `PR2.npz` |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 448 (22.1%) | 69 (3.4%) |
| 1 | 315 (15.6%) | 301 (14.9%) |
| 2 | 659 (32.5%) | 619 (30.6%) |
| 3 | 223 (11.0%) | 1,031 (51.0%) |
| 4 | 298 (14.7%) | 0 |
| 5 | 42 (2.1%) | 0 |
| 6 | 40 (2.0%) | 0 |

Main assigns 18.8% of its records to result ranks 4 through 6. PR2 instead concentrates just over half of its records at rank 3.

### Distinct input shapes by rank

| Input-shape rank | `main.npz` | `PR2.npz` | Possible in PR2's `{0,1,2,3,4}` dimension universe |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 1 | 5 | 5 | 5 |
| 2 | 21 | 25 | 25 |
| 3 | 60 | 124 | 125 |
| 4 | 110 | 0 | Not in scope |
| 5 | 34 | 0 | Not in scope |
| 6 | 38 | 0 | Not in scope |

PR2 covers every possible rank-0, rank-1, and rank-2 input shape using dimensions `{0,1,2,3,4}`. At rank 3 it covers 124 of 125 possibilities; the only absent input shape is `(2, 2, 0)`. That shape does occur as a broadcast result, so PR2 still covers all 156 possible result shapes in its bounded universe.

## Coverage by operand role

| Role | Metric | `main.npz` | `PR2.npz` |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Parameters | Operand occurrences | 3,370 | 3,360 |
| Parameters | Distinct shapes | 13 | 148 |
| Parameters | Scalar occurrences | 1,921 (57.0%) | 1,426 (42.4%) |
| `x` | Operand occurrences | 2,025 | 2,020 |
| `x` | Distinct shapes | 143 | 139 |
| `x` | Scalar occurrences | 929 (45.9%) | 539 (26.7%) |
| `y` | Operand occurrences | 2,025 | 2,020 |
| `y` | Distinct shapes | 219 | 115 |
| `y` | Scalar occurrences | 1,042 (51.5%) | 558 (27.6%) |

The most substantial PR2 improvement is parameter-shape diversity: 148 distinct shapes rather than 13. Main's larger `y` vocabulary is primarily a consequence of permitting ranks 4 through 6.

Across all roles, 52.5% of main's operands are scalar, compared with 34.1% of PR2's operands.

## Broadcasting mechanisms

| Per-record condition | `main.npz` | `PR2.npz` |
|---|---:|---:|
| No broadcasting required | 453 (22.4%) | 76 (3.8%) |
| Implicit leading-axis expansion, without singleton expansion | 872 (43.1%) | 750 (37.1%) |
| Singleton expansion, without implicit leading-axis expansion | 2 (0.1%) | 46 (2.3%) |
| Both mechanisms | 698 (34.5%) | 1,148 (56.8%) |
| Any implicit leading-axis expansion | 1,570 (77.5%) | 1,898 (94.0%) |
| Any singleton expansion | 700 (34.6%) | 1,194 (59.1%) |
| Zero-length dimension present | 728 (36.0%) | 705 (34.9%) |

The four mechanism rows at the top of the table are mutually exclusive and exhaust all records. PR2's main improvement is not merely that it broadcasts more often: it combines rank padding and explicit singleton expansion in 56.8% of records, compared with 34.5% in main.

### Number of operands changed to the result shape

| Changed operands | `main.npz` | `PR2.npz` |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 453 (22.4%) | 76 (3.8%) |
| 1 | 65 (3.2%) | 61 (3.0%) |
| 2 | 451 (22.3%) | 711 (35.2%) |
| 3 | 749 (37.0%) | 798 (39.5%) |
| 4 | 307 (15.2%) | 374 (18.5%) |

Records have either three operands (one parameter, `x`, and `y`) or four operands (two parameters, `x`, and `y`). PR2 changes at least two operands in 1,883 records, or 93.2% of the archive. Main does so in 1,507 records, or 74.4%.

## Selected situations

| Situation | `main.npz` | `PR2.npz` |
|---|---:|---:|
| Same-rank, multidirectional singleton expansion | 12 | 38 |
| Three operands owning different result axes | 3 | 2 |
| Zero against singleton | 359 | 399 |
| All operands scalar | 448 | 69 |

Both archives contain every selected situation. PR2 gives substantially more coverage to same-rank multidirectional expansion and slightly more to explicit zero-versus-singleton broadcasting. Cases in which three operands independently determine three result axes remain rare in both archives.

The all-scalar count is large in main because it includes records associated with different parameter counts and, potentially, different distributions. It should not automatically be interpreted as 448 redundant tests. As shape coverage alone, however, it is heavy repetition of the same baseline condition.

## Dimension values

Counting every explicit axis in every operand:

| Dimension value | `main.npz` | `PR2.npz` |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 1,273 | 1,168 |
| 1 | 4,221 | 4,730 |
| 2 | 1,122 | 1,213 |
| 3 | 304 | 1,270 |
| 4 | 89 | 1,254 |
| 5 | 8 | 0 |

On non-singleton ordinary dimensions, PR2 is much more balanced across sizes 2, 3, and 4. Main is strongly concentrated on size 2 and uses size 5 only eight times. The high frequency of ones in both archives is expected for generators designed to produce mutually broadcastable shapes.

## Assessment

Within ranks 0 through 3, PR2 is the stronger suite by a wide margin. It provides:

- many more exact and structural configurations;
- nearly exhaustive coverage of its intended input-shape universe;
- dramatically broader parameter-shape coverage;
- fewer all-scalar and otherwise non-broadcasting records;
- more cases combining rank padding with explicit singleton expansion; and
- more cases in which several operands change shape simultaneously.

Main remains valuable for a separate reason: high-rank coverage. It has 380 records whose broadcast result has rank 4, 5, or 6, including 82 at ranks 5 and 6. PR2 tests none of these ranks.

If PR2 is intended to replace main entirely, loss of high-rank coverage is the principal regression. If high-rank behavior is not inherently important, PR2 is a clear improvement. If it is important, a compact deterministic supplement of representative rank-4-through-rank-6 configurations would preserve main's distinctive benefit without restoring its heavy scalar duplication.

</details>

title: MAINT: special: dependency on optimize.elementwise closes a large cycle in the tach module graph

labels.name: maintenance
labels.description: Items related to regular maintenance tasks

body:
`tach.toml` declares `scipy.special` as depending on `scipy.optimize.elementwise`. Since `scipy.optimize` in turn depends on `scipy.special`, that edge (together with e.g. `linalg` ↔ `sparse.linalg` and `fft` → `special`) makes the declared module graph one strongly connected component of 21 subpackages: fft, integrate, interpolate, linalg (+blas/lapack/interpolative), ndimage, optimize (+elementwise), sparse (+csgraph, linalg), spatial (+distance, transform), special, stats (+contingency, distributions, qmc).

The `special` → `optimize` edge is the notable one because `special` is otherwise a low-level layer. It comes from a single function-local import:

https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/9b25efba554f5ca0fa00590a7b45ee118fbb8091/scipy/special/_support_alternative_backends.py#L426

```python
from scipy.optimize.elementwise import bracket_root, find_root
```

It is used only by `_stdtrit` on non-NumPy backends to invert `stdtr` by root-finding.

This is deliberate and `tach check --exact` passes, so this isn't a bug. I'm raising it in case it's worth keeping `special` below `optimize` in the layering. Options:
- move the generic elementwise bracketing/root-finding core into `scipy._lib` (where both `special` and `optimize.elementwise` can use it), or
- accept the edge and leave a comment in `tach.toml` explaining why it exists.

**Done when:** either `scipy.special` no longer lists `scipy.optimize.elementwise` in `tach.toml` (with `tach check --exact` passing), or the edge is documented as intended.

title: BUG: energy_distance and wasserstein_distance return 0.0 for highly skewed valid weights (cancellation/underflow)

labels.name: defect
labels.description: A clear bug or issue that prevents SciPy from being installed or used as expected

labels.name: needs-decision
labels.description: Items that need further discussion before they are merged or closed

body:
### Describe your issue.

When computing weighted distances between distributions using extremely small but valid `float64` weights, `energy_distance` and `wasserstein_distance` can incorrectly return `0.0` instead of the true distance. 

For **`energy_distance`**, an intermediate calculation underflows. A related issue for a private helper was raised in #19712 for high powers, but this reproducer shows it affects the public `energy_distance` function at the supported power 2 when input weights have wide dynamic range. 

For **`wasserstein_distance`**, forward CDF accumulation erases the right tail due to rounding. Simply reflecting the distribution changes the distance from `0.0` to `1.0`.

*(Note: As per SciPy's AI policy, I am disclosing that I used an AI coding assistant to help me systematically explore, discover, and isolate this numerical edge case. I have reviewed the math and verified the reproduction scripts locally.)*

### Reproducing Code Example

```python
from scipy.stats import energy_distance, wasserstein_distance

# 1. Energy Distance Underflow
A, w = 2.0**1023, 2.0**-538
print("Energy distance:", energy_distance([-A, 0.0], [0.0], [w, 1.0], [1.0]))
# Observed: 0.0
# Correctly rounded answer: 2**-26 (approx 1.4901161193847656e-8)

# 2. Wasserstein Distance CDF Cancellation
L, p = 2.0**60, 2.0**-60
print("W1 distance (forward):", wasserstein_distance([0.0, L], [0.0], [1.0, p], [1.0]))
print("W1 distance (reversed):", wasserstein_distance([0.0, -L], [0.0], [1.0, p], [1.0]))
# Observed: 0.0, 1.0
# Both exact values should be equal to 1/(1+p), which is near 1.0
```

### Error message

```shell
There is no crash/error message, just an incorrect mathematical result.
```

### SciPy/NumPy/Python version and system information

```shell
Windows 11
Python 3.14.2
NumPy 2.5.3
SciPy 1.18.1
```

title: BUG: io.FortranFile.read_record: cannot read gfortran/Intel subrecords for records > 2GB (4-byte header)

labels.name: defect
labels.description: A clear bug or issue that prevents SciPy from being installed or used as expected

body:
### Describe your issue.

`scipy.io.FortranFile.read_record` cannot read unformatted sequential Fortran files where a single record exceeds 2**31-1 bytes (~2GB) with a 4-byte record-length header. This is the default for gfortran/Intel unless an 8-byte marker is forced via compiler flag. This is already noted in the class docstring:

> "It also does not support the subrecords used in Intel and gfortran
> compilers for records which are greater than 2GB with a 4-byte header."

Still true on `main` as of 2026-09-24. I couldn't find an existing issue or PR tracking it.

When a 4-byte-marker compiler writes a record larger than `INT32_MAX`, gfortran/Intel split it into multiple physical subrecords, each with its own 4-byte header/footer. The header's **sign** is the continuation flag: negative = more subrecords follow, positive = final subrecord. `read_record` has no concept of this, so such files either raise `ValueError: Sizes do not agree in the header and footer for this record` or return wrong/truncated data.

Suggested fix:
Two-pass read:
1. Walk the subrecord chain from the record start, following negative headers and summing payload sizes until a positive header marks the last subrecord, validating each header/footer pair.
2. Seek back and either read directly (single subrecord, unchanged) or concatenate subrecord payloads before interpreting against the requested dtype(s). Single-subrecord files are unaffected.

I have a working reference implementation (a FortranFile subclass, with tests using an artificially split small file, no multi-GB fixture needed) and can adapt it into a PR if welcome.

### Reproducing Code Example

```python
integer(8), parameter :: n = 600000000_8  ! >2GB as real(4)
real(4), allocatable :: a(:)
allocate(a(n)); a = 1.0
open(1, file='big.dat', form='unformatted'); write(1) a; close(1)
! Compiled with plain gfortran (no -frecord-marker=8)


from scipy.io import FortranFile
FortranFile('big.dat').read_record('<f4')
```

### Error message

```shell
ValueError: Sizes do not agree in the header and footer for this record
```

title: TST: restore the matplotlib backend after plotting tests

labels.name: maintenance
labels.description: Items related to regular maintenance tasks

body:
#### Reference issue
Closes gh-3588.

#### What does this implement/fix?
Three test modules (`cluster/hierarchy/tests/test_hierarchy.py`, `spatial/tests/test__plotutils.py` and `stats/tests/test_morestats.py`) set matplotlib's backend to Agg at import time. So after running the tests in a session the process is left on Agg and the user's plots stop showing up, which is what gh-3588 describes.

I went with the fixture pv suggested on the issue: `mpl_agg` in `scipy/conftest.py` switches to Agg for a plotting test, closes the figures and switches back afterwards. I made it function-scoped so each test cleans up after itself. The import-time switches are removed from the three modules and the 11 plotting tests get `@pytest.mark.usefixtures("mpl_agg")`.

One thing to be aware of: the fixture restores whatever backend was resolved before the test. Matplotlib doesn't offer a public way back to the unresolved "auto" state. And if the previous backend can't be re-activated (say a GUI backend on a headless box) it just stays on Agg, which is what happens on main today anyway.

#### Additional information
I checked this in-process with `pytest.main` on headless Linux (matplotlib 3.11.2). With `MPLBACKEND=svg` the backend is `svg` after the run (on main it's `Agg`); with it unset you end on `agg`; `TkAgg` or a bogus `module://` value don't error and end on Agg; an invalid value makes the plotting tests skip instead of erroring at collection.

I don't have a machine with a GUI toolkit, so if someone with a display could run the plotting tests with `MPLBACKEND` unset and check `matplotlib.get_backend()` afterwards, that would be really helpful.

A few things I left out to keep this small — happy to do them here or separately if you'd like: marking the `mpl_agg` tests `thread_unsafe` for pytest-run-parallel (pyplot's figure registry isn't thread-safe; the parallel CI job doesn't install matplotlib), a subprocess regression test, and `stats/tests/test_continuous.py::test_plot` / `stats/tests/test_survival.py`, which also create figures without the fixture.

title: Tracking issue: custom methods for continuous distributions

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: A new feature or improvement

labels.name: task

body:
## Before submitting a PR regarding this issue

_This issue is strongly affected by current efforts to update the distribution infrastructure (see #15928). The infrastructure update will improve the precision and performance of all distribution methods. Until this new infrastructure is in place, new function overrides are unlikely to be accepted. You are welcome to look into other distribution related issues though._

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

Continuous distributions in `scipy` expose (among others) the following [methods](https://output.circle-artifacts.com/output/job/d1b78493-3718-4ce8-bc14-6793988341f5/artifacts/0/html/reference/generated/scipy.stats.rv_continuous.html#scipy.stats.rv_continuous): 

```shell
_rvs (generate random samples)
_pdf (probability density function)
_logpdf (log of probability density function)
_cdf (cumulative probability density function)
_logcdf (log of cumulative probability density function)
_sf (survival function, 1 - CDF)
_ppf (percentile function, inverse of CDF)
_isf (inverse survival function)
_stats (first 4 moments)
_munp (moment generating function)
_entropy (differential entropy)
fit (fitting the distribution parameters given data)
```

The only necessary method though is `_pdf` or `_cdf` . If one of them is given, the other methods can be derived using generic default methods by the distribution infrastructure.

For example, the survival function is by default calculated as `sf=1 - _cdf`. This comes with the risk of catastrophic cancellations in the right tail of distributions as we practically do `1 - (almost) 1`. Random variate generation (`rvs`) falls back to inverse transform sampling using the percentile function `_ppf`. If `_ppf` is expensive or imprecise to compute, `rvs` becomes very slow.

All in all, these default methods can result in imprecise and slow results. Therefore, distributions often override the default methods. Examples for the benefits are:

* #17708 : a custom `_ppf` method for the `genexpon` distribution resulted in more than a 1000x speedup for generating samples
* #15360 : a custom `_rvs` method for the `nakagami` distribution resulted in a 20x speedup for generating samples
* #17742 : a custom `_entropy` method enables to reliably calculate the differential entropy for the `chi` and `chi2` distribution where the fallback default implementation fails


One note regarding difficulty levels: if an analytical formula can be found for a function, this often looks straight forward to implement. Still, SciPy seeks to maintain high precision also for extreme values. For that reason, many implementations make extensive use of functions from `scipy.special`. Please have a look at examples for other distributions when you approach these. Implementing a `fit` method is probably the most difficult method to work on but also the one with the greatest benefit compared to the default implementation.

### Describe the solution you'd like.

@WarrenWeckesser maintains a script that scans the scipy code base and returns distributions missing custom methods: https://github.com/WarrenWeckesser/analyze-scipy-code/blob/main/dists_that_override.py

I propose to update the list here to track improvements and give contributors a possibility to quickly discover an issue to work on.

The script marks overridden methods with a checkmark. Many not checkmarked methods could potentially be improved. Current output (last update: 17-August-2024) using `python dists_that_override.py _rvs _logpdf _cdf _ppf _sf _isf fit _stats _munp _entropy`:

title: BUG: stats.mannwhitneyu: method='auto' makes an untied slice's p-value depend on ties in other slices

labels.name: defect
labels.description: A clear bug or issue that prevents SciPy from being installed or used as expected

labels.name: needs-decision
labels.description: Items that need further discussion before they are merged or closed

body:
### Describe your issue.

I observed that, for NumPy float64 arrays without NaNs, the p-value of an untied slice returned by `mannwhitneyu` with `method='auto'` and `axis=-1` depends on whether another slice contains ties.

Here, ties mean repeated values within the pooled pair of samples for an individual slice, not equal values appearing in different slices.

When either sample size is at most 8, the implementation I inspected chooses `exact` or `asymptotic` for the entire call based on whether any slice contains ties. Consequently, replacing separate calls in a loop with a single call using `axis` can change a slice's p-value even though that slice's own inputs have not changed.

I expected each slice's result to agree with a separate call. This expectation is related to the multidimensional input support discussed in [gh-12837](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/12837) and [gh-11113](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/11113), but I would like to clarify whether it also applies to automatic method selection.

For the untied target slice below, using a two-sided test with continuity correction enabled, U is 5:

```python
x = [0, 1, 2, 3, 9]
y = [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11]
```

| Call | Target slice's p-value |
| --- | --- |
| Alone, `method='auto'` | `0.04797979797979798` |
| Batched with another untied slice, `method='auto'` | `0.04797979797979798` |
| Batched with a slice containing one tied pair, `method='auto'` | `0.05131990358807116` |
| Alone, `method='exact'` | `0.04797979797979798` |
| Alone, `method='asymptotic'` | `0.05131990358807116` |

The target slice's inputs, sample sizes, and U are unchanged. The p-value crosses 0.05, changing this slice's decision at the 5% significance level. Reversing the rows of the batched input does not change the target slice's result. No multiple-testing correction is applied.

This behavior was observed with both SciPy `1.18.1` and development build `2.0.0.dev0+git20260902.fb96fc6`, with NumPy `2.3.5` at runtime in both environments.

For the untied target slice, enumerating all 792 rank allocations gives an inclusive two-sided exact probability of `38/792 = 19/396`. A separate implementation of the continuity-corrected normal approximation also agrees with the asymptotic value above. Both p-values are therefore consistent with their respective methods in this example. The concern is the choice of method for a slice changing because another slice contains ties, rather than an arithmetic error in the approximation.

In the inspected source, the method is selected by:

```python
_mwu_choose_method(n1, n2, xp.any(t > 1))
```

Because `xp.any(t > 1)` reduces over all axes, a tie in any slice selects `asymptotic` for the entire call. The asymptotic tie correction, however, is computed separately for each slice:

```python
xp.sum(t**3 - t, axis=-1)
```

This distinguishes the observed method-selection effect from another slice's tie correction being incorporated into the target slice's variance. The target slice's p-value in the mixed batch agrees with its standalone `method='asymptotic'` result.

It was not clear to me whether the docstring's “there are no ties” refers to each slice or the entire input. The latter interpretation would be consistent with the implementation.

In the tests I inspected, `test_gh_12837_11113` compares batched and separate calls but parametrizes only `exact` and `asymptotic`; `test_auto` uses one-dimensional inputs. Testing this case requires an explicit mixture of tied and untied slices, rather than just adding `auto` to the existing method parametrization.

A similar global tie check appears in the historical implementation in [gh-4933](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/4933). I have not checked every intervening version, so this is not an exhaustive regression analysis. I did not find a report directly addressing this cross-slice p-value dependency within the tracker material I reviewed.

For context, the Wilcoxon discussion in [gh-21567](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/21567) notes that `nan_policy='omit'` can produce different sample sizes across slices, allowing `auto` to choose different methods. That concerns a different test and input condition; I do not take it as defining the intended Mann–Whitney U behavior here.

**Question**

Is selecting one method for all slices based on ties anywhere in the input intentional?

- If so, could the `method` docstring explicitly explain that ties in another slice can change the selected method and p-value? Guidance on choosing an appropriate method for each slice would also help users who need agreement with separate calls. I am not suggesting applying `method='exact'` indiscriminately to tied slices, since it does not correct for ties.
- If per-slice automatic selection is the intended behavior, a test comparing separate and batched calls with an explicit mixture of tied and untied slices would cover this case.

I am not proposing a particular implementation. I have not measured how often this occurs in practice or its effects on Type I or Type II error rates.

**AI assistance**

I wrote the outline, drafted the text in Japanese, developed and executed the reproducer, performed the mathematical cross-checks, and inspected the source code and tracker myself. AI assistance was used only to translate the Japanese draft into English.

### Reproducing Code Example

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import mannwhitneyu

# Target slice A: no ties within the pooled sample.
x = np.array([0, 1, 2, 3, 9], dtype=np.float64)
y = np.array([4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11], dtype=np.float64)

# Companion slice B: initially untied.
bx = x + 20
by = y + 20
bx_tied = bx.copy()
bx_tied[1] = bx_tied[0]  # Introduce one tied pair within B only.

options = dict(
    axis=-1,
    alternative="two-sided",
    use_continuity=True,
    nan_policy="propagate",
)

single = mannwhitneyu(x, y, method="auto", **options)
untied_batch = mannwhitneyu(
    np.stack([x, bx]), np.stack([y, by]), method="auto", **options
)
mixed_batch = mannwhitneyu(
    np.stack([x, bx_tied]), np.stack([y, by]), method="auto", **options
)
exact = mannwhitneyu(x, y, method="exact", **options)
asymptotic = mannwhitneyu(x, y, method="asymptotic", **options)
reversed_batch = mannwhitneyu(
    np.stack([bx_tied, x]), np.stack([by, y]), method="auto", **options
)

# Report A only; A is the second row in reversed_batch.
print("single auto:", single.statistic, single.pvalue)
print("untied batch A:", untied_batch.statistic[0], untied_batch.pvalue[0])
print("mixed batch A:", mixed_batch.statistic[0], mixed_batch.pvalue[0])
print("single exact:", exact.statistic, exact.pvalue)
print("single asymptotic:", asymptotic.statistic, asymptotic.pvalue)
print("reversed mixed batch A:", reversed_batch.statistic[1], reversed_batch.pvalue[1])
```

### Error message


title: BUG: optimize.shgo: correctly reorder X_min in sort_min_pool

labels.name: defect
labels.description: A clear bug or issue that prevents SciPy from being installed or used as expected

body:
**Context / Note for Maintainers**
Supersedes #25881 and re-submits the complete fix. Following up on the previous PR discussion: the author of #25881 remained unresponsive after a week, and #25881 is incomplete as detailed below.

**Reference issue**
Closes gh-25838

**What does this implement/fix?**
This fixes a bug in SHGO.sort_min_pool() where self.X_min was not being reordered alongside self.minimizer_pool and self.minimizer_pool_F.

**The Problem:** Because X_min remained in raw discovery order while the other pool arrays were sorted by function value ascending, minimise_pool() passed mismatched (x0, ind) pairs (starting local searches from raw X_min[0] while labeling them with the sorted minimizer_pool[0]). This caused options like local_iter=N to evaluate arbitrary points instead of the best ones.

**Why #25881 is incomplete:** In #25881, removing np.ravel() causes np.argsort() to return a 2D index matrix (N, 1) whenever minimizer_pool_F is 2D. Slicing X_min with a 2D matrix distorts array dimensions, triggering downstream AssertionErrors during full runs.

**The Fix:**

Reorders self.X_min using self.ind_f_min inside sort_min_pool().

Preserves np.ravel() to ensure proper 1D indexing.

Adds defensive ravel statements and reshape guards to prevent broadcasting/shape mismatch errors during edge-case optimization runs.

Adds a regression test ensuring X_min correctly tracks the sorted order of minimizer_pool_F.

**Additional information**
Verified locally using:
Bash
spin test -t scipy.optimize.tests.test__shgo

title: BUG: stats.yeojohnson: return lmbda=1 for arbitrary constant inputs

labels.name: defect
labels.description: A clear bug or issue that prevents SciPy from being installed or used as expected

body:
#### Description

This PR fixes an issue in `scipy.stats.yeojohnson_normmax` where passing a constant 1D array results in arbitrary and extreme optimal λ values.

When applying the Yeo-Johnson transform to constant data, the variance is zero regardless of the λ applied. Because the log-likelihood calculation includes the logarithm of the variance, that part of the equation evaluates to negative infinity (making the likelihood undefined) for any λ. The optimizer ends up chasing floating-point rounding errors during these operations, leading to silent numerical explosions. For example:

* Constant `4` →λ≈76.7, transformed values ≈ `5e51`
* Constant `1000` → transformed values ≈ `3e100`
* Constant `-3` →λ≈−43.5

To resolve this safely, this PR generalizes the existing fallback mechanism. Previously, `yeojohnson_normmax` explicitly checked for arrays of all zeros and returned λ=1. This check has now been broadened to apply to any constant array.

Returning λ=1 is the safest default, as it reduces the transform to the identity function, leaving the constant inputs unchanged. While the sibling function `boxcox` raises an error on constant data, SciPy already has backward-compatibility tests relying on `yeojohnson_normmax([0, 0, 0])` returning a finite value. Expanding this fallback fixes the bug without introducing breaking changes.

(Note for maintainers: If the preference is to align strictly with `boxcox` and raise a `ValueError` for all constant arrays, including zeros, I am happy to update the PR).

#### Modifications & Testing

* Updated `yeojohnson_normmax` to check for equality against the first element instead of zero.
* Verified that `nan_policy='omit'` works seamlessly: since NaNs are already stripped before the constant check, constant arrays with NaNs naturally return λ=1 without requiring extra logic.
* Added parameterized tests for `yeojohnson` and `yeojohnson_normmax` covering various constants (`-3`, `0.001`, `1`, `4`, `1000`).
* Added tests asserting that the transformed array is identical to the input array (tested on cases without NaNs).
* Added a test verifying that λ=1 is correctly returned for a constant input containing a NaN.

#### Reference issue

None

Claude Code discovered this bug while running SciPy on real data, analyzed the root cause, and wrote the code for the fix, the tests, and the commit message. The English text of this PR description was drafted with Claude (claude.ai) and reviewed by me. labels.name: Documentation

body:
`var` accumulates `d_k**2` over the steps actually taken, so it only equals the diagonals of `(A'A + damp^2*I)^{-1}` once the bidiagonalization has run the full `n` steps. `lsqr` stops as soon as `x` meets the tolerances, usually much earlier, so `var` is normally an underestimate. Even at `n` steps the estimate degrades with problem size because the bidiagonalization vectors lose orthogonality. Measurements are in #22232.

Documents that, and adds a regression test pinning `var` against the exact diagonals for a small problem run to `n` steps.

Closes #22232
