#### Reference issue
Towards gh-23315

Depends on:
- gh-24622
- gh-24627
- gh-24669
- gh-24745

TODO:
- [x] batched tests
- [x] update docs
- [ ] benchmarking for the forum

Follow-up:
- the other solvers: gh-24926
- JIT support: gh-24956 

#### Context

This PR is part of work towards adding batching and array API standard support across the different iterative sparse linear solvers in `sparse.linalg`, tracked in gh-23315. There have been quite a few PRs leading up to this, primarily adding batching and array API support to the data structure which these solvers use, https://scipy.github.io/devdocs/reference/generated/scipy.sparse.linalg.LinearOperator.html. Future PRs will extend the work done here for `cg` to other solvers like `bicgstab` and `qmr`.

The rough idea behind the batching is touched on in https://discuss.scientific-python.org/t/batching-linearoperator-status-and-benchmarks/2199 — we iterate through the entire batch until every system has converged (or we hit `maxiter` etc.). We mask out converged systems in some places to try to avoid too much superfluous computation or divergence-after-convergence. This is expected to yield benefits for large batches of systems where vectorising the `matvec` function is efficient and each system in the batch takes a similar amount of iterations to converge. It is assumed to not do much better than serial calls when a vectorised matvec is not much faster, for small batches, or when a single system can take many more iterations than another in the batch.

My plan is to go back to the forum with benchmarking results once we are happy that the implementation and tests look solid here. https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/24745#issuecomment-4075915712 shows promise for at least one problem vs batched dense solvers, with significant memory benefits and performance benefits for large batches of small-to-medium matrices. https://discuss.scientific-python.org/t/batching-linearoperator-status-and-benchmarks/2199 shows promise for large batches of smaller batched sparse and dense systems vs using the existing `cg` serially.

Use-case for multiclass ridge classification over a grid of `alpha`: https://github.com/lucascolley/ridge-batched-cg/blob/main/batched-cg.ipynb

title: BUG: Intermittent SIGSEGV in Accelerate-backed positive-definite solves on macOS 27 RC; native DPOTRF reproducer

labels.name: defect
labels.description: A clear bug or issue that prevents SciPy from being installed or used as expected

body:
### Describe your issue

On an Apple M4 Pro running macOS 27.0 RC (build 26A428), an 84-process stress of `scipy.linalg.cho_factor(lower=False)` and `scipy.linalg.solve(assume_a="pos")` on well-conditioned symmetric positive-definite matrices produced two SIGSEGV exits with conda-forge SciPy 1.17.1 linked to Accelerate. The same script completed 84/84 processes after switching only the BLAS/LAPACK provider back to OpenBLAS.

This may be an upstream Accelerate defect: a standalone C call to Accelerate's `dpotrf_`, with no Python or SciPy, also segfaults for selected sizes when run under Apple's GuardMalloc. I am reporting the SciPy-visible failure and native reproducer for diagnosis; these results do **not** establish a SciPy wrapper bug. I have not tested SciPy main or the latest release on this host.

Observed Python failures in one complete run:

- n=2048, `solve(assume_a="pos")`, RNG seed 2: return code -11, empty stderr.
- n=2048, `cho_factor(lower=False)`, RNG seed 9: return code -11, stderr below.

The failures are intermittent; a single successful execution is not a reliable negative result. Matrices are `M @ M.T + n*I`, explicitly symmetrized. The test uses one native thread. A separate 84-process test of `np.linalg.cholesky` followed by `scipy.linalg.cho_solve((L, True), B)` completed without crashes and passed residual checks; that is a bounded observation rather than a general safety claim.

### Reproducing Code Example

```python
import subprocess, sys, os
CASE = r"""
import sys, numpy as np, scipy.linalg as sla
n, mode, seed = int(sys.argv[1]), sys.argv[2], int(sys.argv[3])
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed); M = rng.standard_normal((n, n)); A = M @ M.T + n*np.eye(n); A = 0.5*(A+A.T)
if mode == "posv": sla.solve(A, np.ones((n,2)), assume_a="pos")
else: sla.cho_factor(A, lower=False)
"""
env = dict(os.environ, VECLIB_MAXIMUM_THREADS="1", OMP_NUM_THREADS="1")
crashes = 0; total = 0
for seed in range(14):
```

title: ENH: mparray: support arbitrary precision array backend

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: A new feature or improvement

labels.name: array types
labels.description: Items related to array API support and input array validation (see gh-18286)

labels.name: needs-release-note
labels.description: A maintainer should add a release note written by a reviewer/author to the wiki.

body:
#### Reference issue
Toward gh-15928 ("The infrastructure supports non-NumPy arrays (e.g. CuPy) and NumPy arrays that support nonstandard numerical types (e.g. mpmath).")

#### What does this implement/fix?
This begins to test functions written in terms of the array API standard against [`mparray`](https://github.com/mdhaber/mparray), an array backend that uses `mpmath` (and Python `int`s) to perform arbitrary precision calculations.

Extra precision may not be essential for typical calculations, but:
- it will be useful to avoid under/overflow when our usual implementation is not yet robust
- it will be useful for generating reference values for test with tight tolerances
- it will be useful when the new distribution infrastructure is array API compatible and users need high precision
- it will "just work" for functions written in terms of the array API standard; there should be no need for special treatment (like there is for JAX JIT or MArray). We would *not* consider it supported unless the whole calculation were written in terms of the array API standard (e.g. no conversion to NumPy arrays and back allowed).

```python3
import mparray as xp
from mpmath import mp
mp.dps = 30
from scipy import stats

# follows dtype promotion rules to statisfy array API tests, but all calculations are arbitrary precision
xp.asarray([xp.pi, xp.e], dtype=xp.float32)
# MPArray([mpf('3.14159265358979311599796346854419'), mpf('2.71828182845904509079559829842765')], dtype=float32)

# uses Python ints for arbitrary size integers
xp.asarray([2**70, 2**100], dtype=int)
# MPArray([1180591620717411303424, 1267650600228229401496703205376], dtype=int64)

# will "just work" with functions written in terms of the array API standard
x = xp.asarray([1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 10, 12, 11, 15], dtype=float)

stats.skew(x)  # MPArray(mpf('0.121491721105814996108126923872303'), dtype=float64)

res = stats.ttest_1samp(x, 0)
res.statistic  # MPArray(mpf('4.62895319021822725322316817045339'), dtype=float64)
res.pvalue  # MPArray(mpf('0.0016903539065257161631145033098278'), dtype=float64)
```

#### Additional information
@steppi Unlike `marray`, this *would* be treated as a typical backend for the sake of testing and documentation, but it would probably require a lot less work if the `xp_capabilities` tables were opt-in (rather than opt-out like other backends). Thoughts on whether we should go that route and if so, how?

`mparray` now passes ~~most~~essentially all of the `array-api-tests` tests, so I thought it was time to give this a shot. ~~(One important source of failures is `ZeroDivisionError`s raised by `mpmath`; it needs to be overridden to produce `inf`s and `nan`s as appropriate.) `mparray` is not yet released on PyPI, but it can be installed with `pip` from the source directory.~~ `mparray` is available on PyPI and conda-forge.

#### AI Generation Disclosure
No AI

### Describe your issue.

In addition to the known failure of `test_nan_inputs[sph_harm]` on riscv64 (see [issue #22753](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/22753)), we are observing several tests that randomly hang when running under riscv64 in a QEMU-emulated environment. Some of these hangs appear to be related to the use of multiprocessing in combination with QEMU and the fork() system call:

-  test_nan_inputs[sph_harm]
-  test_quad_vec_pool
-  test_quad_vec_pool_args
-  test_19_parallelization

title: BUG: optimize: initialise iterations before the early exits

labels.name: defect
labels.description: A clear bug or issue that prevents SciPy from being installed or used as expected

labels.name: C/C++
labels.description: Items related to the internal C/C++ code base

body:
#### Reference issue

Closes gh-25955.

#### What does this implement/fix?

`bisect`, `ridder`, `brentq` and `brenth` set `solver_stats->iterations` only *after* the checks for an endpoint being a root and for the bracket not changing sign. Those exits return with the field never written, so `root_scalar` reports whatever the struct happened to hold.

The initialisation moves next to `error_num = INPROGRESS`, so it is set on every path out of the function.

#### Additional information

The issue reports wild values. What I see on 1.18.0 is worse in a quieter way — a plausible small count left behind by an earlier call. Running an interior root first, then an endpoint root, makes it deterministic:

```python
from scipy import optimize
def f(x): return x**3 - 1

for m in ['brentq', 'brenth', 'bisect', 'ridder', 'toms748']:
    interior = optimize.root_scalar(f, bracket=(0.5, 10.0), method=m).iterations
    endpoint = optimize.root_scalar(f, bracket=(1.0, 10.0), method=m).iterations
    print(f"{m:8s} interior={interior:3d}  endpoint={endpoint:3d}")
```

```
brentq   interior= 11  endpoint=  6
brenth   interior= 10  endpoint=  6
bisect   interior= 43  endpoint=  6
ridder   interior=  9  endpoint=  6
toms748  interior=  6  endpoint=  0
```

All four report `6`, which is `toms748`'s count from the previous loop iteration — a different solver's leftover. `toms748` is pure Python and already reports 0.

I do not have a Fortran toolchain here, so rather than guess I compiled the four files in `scipy/optimize/Zeros/` standalone against `zeros.h` and called them directly, with the stats struct filled with `0xAB` beforehand:

```
                          brentq  brenth  bisect  ridder
before, endpoint root  -1414812757  (same)  (same)  (same)
after,  endpoint root            0       0       0       0
before, interior root           11      10      43       9
after,  interior root           11      10      43       9
```

So the counts for brackets that actually iterate are untouched; only the early exits change. The `SIGNERR` exit is covered by the same move.

#### Tests

`test_gh_25955_iterations_when_endpoint_is_root` in `scipy/optimize/tests/test_zeros.py`, parametrised over `bracket_methods` and over which endpoint is the root. It runs an iterating bracket first so a stale count is present to be read.

I could not run scipy's own suite locally for the reason above, so I ran the test body against released 1.18.0 to confirm it distinguishes the two states: **8 of 10 parameter combinations fail**, and the two `toms748` cases pass, which is the expected split.

#### AI Generation Disclosure

Claude (Opus 5) was used. It searched the four C files for the ordering problem after I read the issue, drafted the one-line move in each and the test, and wrote this description. I checked each diff, built and ran the standalone C harness above to confirm the before/after numbers myself, and confirmed the test fails against released scipy. The changed C is four identical single-line moves; the test is mine to explain and I am happy to take questions on it.

title: BUG: initialize bracketing solver iteration counts

labels.name: defect
labels.description: A clear bug or issue that prevents SciPy from being installed or used as expected

labels.name: C/C++
labels.description: Items related to the internal C/C++ code base

body:
#### Reference issue
Closes gh-25955.

#### What does this implement/fix?
`bisect`, `brentq`, `brenth`, and `ridder` (the C bracketing solvers backing
`scipy.optimize.root_scalar`) returned as soon as they detected that one
bracket endpoint was already a root, but `solver_stats->iterations` was only
initialized to 0 *after* that early-return check, inside the main iteration
loop. When a bracket endpoint was itself the root, the function returned
before that initialization ran, so `iterations` was left holding whatever
value happened to be in that stack memory, and Python-level callers using
`full_output=True` could observe an uninitialized/garbage iteration count for
an otherwise valid, zero-iteration result.

This moves `solver_stats->iterations = 0` up to just after `error_num` is set
at the top of each function, before the endpoint checks, so it is always
initialized regardless of which return path is taken. The iteration-counting
logic in the main loop is unchanged. `toms748` was not touched because it
already initializes/returns zero iterations correctly in this case.

#### Additional information
Added a regression test in `scipy/optimize/tests/test_zeros.py` parametrized
over `brentq`, `brenth`, `bisect`, and `ridder`, and over which bracket
endpoint (0 or 1) is the root, asserting the correct root is returned and
`iterations == 0`.

Verified locally: full `scipy/optimize/tests/test_zeros.py` suite passes
(178 passed) against a rebuilt wheel with the affected C extension rebuilt.

Claude Code (Anthropic) was used as a coding assistant to help diagnose the
uninitialized-memory bug, implement the fix in the four C solver files, write
the regression test, and prepare this pull request description. All changes

Many of the functions in scipy do not include examples in their docstrings.  Even a simple example can be helpful for a new user, so we should try to include examples wherever possible.

title: BUG:stats.kruskal: count the samples before promoting them

#### Reference issue

None; found while reading the array-API promotion path.

#### What does this implement/fix?

`kruskal` and `f_oneway` take `len(samples)` after `xp_promote`, which returns a
bare array for a lone argument, so the length read is that array's rows. A single

promotion fixes both, as `obrientransform` already does.

These are the only two sites in `scipy/stats` taking `len()` of the name
`xp_promote` assigned.

title: CI/DEV: allow forks to opt in to running workflows via a repository variable

labels.name: CI
labels.description: Items related to the CI tools such as CircleCI, GitHub Actions or Azure

labels.name: DX
labels.description: Everything related to making the experience of working on SciPy more pleasant

body:
15 of the 17 workflows in `.github/workflows/` are guarded by `if: github.repository == 'scipy/scipy'` (e.g. `lint.yml`, `linux.yml`, `macos.yml`, `windows.yml`). This is a sensible default: it keeps forks from burning Actions minutes on a full matrix. But it also means a contributor who *wants* CI on their fork can't turn it on without editing every workflow, and a fork that tracks `main` has no CI signal of its own.

**Proposal:** an opt-in repository variable, e.g.

```yaml
if: github.repository == 'scipy/scipy' || vars.SCIPY_FORK_CI == 'true'
```

applied at least to the cheap jobs (`lint.yml`, and perhaps one Linux job in `linux.yml`). Default behaviour on forks is unchanged. A fork owner sets the variable in their repo settings to opt in.

**Done when:** setting `SCIPY_FORK_CI=true` on a fork makes the lint workflow (and optionally one Linux test job) run on push/PR there, and unset forks behave exactly as today.

title: BUG: ``special.assoc_legendre_p`` with ``diff_n=2`` return wrong sign at ``z=-1`` for odd degree ``n``

labels.name: defect
labels.description: A clear bug or issue that prevents SciPy from being installed or used as expected

title: BUG: cKDTree.sparse_distance_matrix warns about coo_matrix built internally

labels.name: defect

body:
### Describe your issue.

`cKDTree.sparse_distance_matrix` emits a `DeprecationWarning` about `coo_matrix`, a temporary container that it builds internally and never returns. With the default `output_type='dok_matrix'` two warnings fire: one for the returned `dok_matrix`, which is expected, and one for the internal `coo_matrix`, which the caller cannot see or influence.

`spmatrix.__init__` skips frames under `scipy/sparse`, so the warning is attributed to the first frame outside it.  In this case that is `scipy/spatial/_ckdtree.pyx`, and the warning ends up on the user's call site naming a class they never used. `output_type='dok_array'` silences both warnings, but raises `ValueError: Invalid output type` on 1.15, 1.16 and 1.17 (tested on each).

Projects supporting scipy >= 1.15 have no single code path that works across supported versions and stays quiet under `-W error`.

Found in scikit-image's nightly test against scipy 2.0.0.dev0, where it fails 18 tests that never touch sparse matrices: https://github.com/scikit-image/scikit-image/actions/runs/31940397346/job/95148603504

Expected: only the returned type warns. Internal containers should not.

### Reproducing Code Example

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.spatial import cKDTree
tree = cKDTree(np.array([[0.0, 0.0], [1.0, 1.0]]))
tree.sparse_distance_matrix(tree, max_distance=3.0)  # warns about coo_matrix
```

body:
Fixes #26149

Sparse `sum()` method with `dtype` and `out` specified and `axis=0` does not return the `out` object when the requested `dtype` does not agree with `out.dtype`.  It should match numpy behavior: cast to the requested dtype before the sum occurs, put the result into `out` and return the `out` object. This broken corner case was due to PR #24496 and so was released in 1.18. So it should be backported in a future minor release if one occurs.

In this PR I added two commits: a test to reveal the bug and then the fix to enable the test to pass. The test also checks that `axis=1` works correct (it works fine on main) and checks both int and float dtypes to ensure the casting occurs before the sum which is followed by storing into `out`.

title: BUG: handle single coefficient in cspline1d_eval/qspline1d_eval

labels.name: defect
labels.description: A clear bug or issue that prevents SciPy from being installed or used as expected

body:
#### Reference issue
Closes gh-25090.

#### What does this implement/fix?
`cspline1d_eval` and `qspline1d_eval` evaluate a spline outside its knot
range `[0, N-1]` (where `N = len(cj)`) using mirror-symmetric recursion to
fold the query point back into range. When the coefficient array has only
one element (`N == 1`), that range degenerates to a single point `[0, 0]`,
so the mirror never folds the point back in range and the recursion never
terminates, raising `RecursionError`.

For a single coefficient the spline is constant at every coordinate, so this
adds a special case that fills the result with that coefficient and returns
directly, bypassing the recursive mirroring for `N == 1`. This matches what
the general (non-mirrored) evaluation formula already produces at `N == 1`
via the B-spline basis functions' partition-of-unity property, so it does
not change the function's existing semantics for any other input.

While diagnosing the issue in `cspline1d_eval`, I found the identical
mirror-recursion structure, and therefore the identical `RecursionError` bug,
in the sibling function `qspline1d_eval` (not covered by the original issue
report). Since both functions share the same underlying defect, this PR
fixes both.

#### Additional information
Added regression tests to `scipy/signal/tests/test_bsplines.py` for both
`cspline1d_eval` and `qspline1d_eval`, evaluating a single-coefficient spline
at negative, zero, and positive coordinates.

Verified locally against a wheel built from this branch:
`pytest --pyargs scipy.signal.tests.test_bsplines` (42 passed), plus a manual
reproduction confirming both functions return the constant coefficient value
instead of raising `RecursionError`.

#### AI Generation Disclosure
Claude Code (Anthropic) assisted with bug diagnosis and test execution. The
code and tests were primarily written and reviewed by the human contributor,
who verified all results before submission.

title: BUG: signal: fix RecursionError in cspline1d_eval/qspline1d_eval for N=1

labels.name: defect
labels.description: A clear bug or issue that prevents SciPy from being installed or used as expected

body:
## Summary

`cspline1d_eval` and `qspline1d_eval` hit infinite recursion when the coefficient array has length 1 and evaluation points are negative.

**Root cause:** The mirror-symmetry recursion reflects negative points to positive (`-newx`), but with N=1 the positive point exceeds N-1=0, triggering the other reflection (`2*(N-1) - newx = -newx`), bouncing back to negative indefinitely.

**Fix:** For N=1, the spline is a constant function (the single coefficient value everywhere) under mirror-symmetric boundary conditions. Return `cj[0]` early. Applied to both `cspline1d_eval` and `qspline1d_eval`.

```python
>>> from scipy.signal import cspline1d_eval
>>> cspline1d_eval(np.array([1.0]), np.array([-0.1]))  # Before: RecursionError
array([1.])  # After: correct
```

Closes #25090.

**AI disclosure:** This fix was developed with AI assistance.

title: ENH: interpolate.make_smoothing_spline: support GCV algorithm for user defined knots

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: A new feature or improvement

body:
#### Reference issue
Part 2 of gh-25862. That PR added support for user-provided knots `t` with an explicit `lam`, this one adds automatic `lam` selection via GCV, so `lam=None` works for user knots the same way it does for the default knots.

#### What does this implement/fix?
This PR adapts the Generalized Cross Validation algorithm for the case when user passes the knot vector. The previous GCV path assumed that knots are always at the data sites. This PR implements the general case of the GCV algorithm
implementing the formulas defined in [this](https://github.com/aadya940/scipy-bspline-testing/blob/main/B_Splines_with_arbitary_knots-gcv.pdf) companion report Section 12.

#### Additional information

**Design**
- The search is scale-free. We compute the scale `r = tr(XᵀWX) / tr(Ω)` and minimize the GCV criterion over `s = log10(lam / r)` in a fixed bounded window, instead of searching `lam` directly.
- Rescaling `x` or `y` rescales the selected `lam` by exactly the right factor and returns the same spline.
- The window edges match the two failure extremes of the linear system: below it the penalty is under the roundoff of the data term, above it the system is numerically singular. This also avoids the failures of linear-scale search discussed in gh-23472.

**Implementation**
- The influence-matrix trace is computed from the banded Cholesky factor using de Hoog's formula, so each evaluation of the criterion is `O(m)`. No dense inverse is formed.
- Upper-banded (LAPACK) storage is used throughout the user-knots path.
- Solver failures inside the search propagate as `LinAlgError`.
- TODO left in the code: estimate the condition number via LAPACK `dpbcon` once it is wrapped in `scipy.linalg` (separate follow-up PR later).

**Tests**
- Main test: knots at all data sites must reproduce the default GCV path.
- Grid-argmin check of the GCV criterion.
- Auto-selection compared against R's `smooth.spline` with forced knots.
- Weighted data.
- Scale-invariance at scales from `3e-6` to `1e6`.

title: DOC: wilcoxon test and precision when detecting zeros

labels.name: Documentation
labels.description: Issues related to the SciPy documentation. Also check https://github.com/scipy/scipy.org

body:
### Describe your issue.

Some time ago I reported [a bug in R's `wilcox.test`](https://bugs.r-project.org/show_bug.cgi?id=19071), which also seem to happen in Scipy's `stats.wilcoxon`.

The issue is that [the code for checking the presence of zeros](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/54ef5423f2e4376230ec3bfda6912a07a50958e3/scipy/stats/_wilcoxon.py#L127) checks for exact zeros:

```py
n_zero = xp.count_nonzero(d == 0, axis=None)
```

As a consequence, any minor deviation from zero due to numerical precision will not be detected as a zero and will get a rank assigned by the test, biasing the test statistic.

For example, I'd expect the following to detect the presence of a zero. The first one does because it's exact, but the next two do not and they give different test statistics because one zero is taken as positive and the other as negative (I set `alternative='greater'` just for clarity when calculating the test statistic):

```py
>>> sp.stats.wilcoxon([10, 20, 30, 0], alternative='greater') # exact zero, success
WilcoxonResult(statistic=np.float64(6.0), pvalue=np.float64(0.125))
>>> sp.stats.wilcoxon([10, 20, 30, 1e-100], alternative='greater') # approximate zero, fail
WilcoxonResult(statistic=np.float64(10.0), pvalue=np.float64(0.0625))
>>> sp.stats.wilcoxon([10, 20, 30, -1e-100], alternative='greater') # approximate zero, fail
WilcoxonResult(statistic=np.float64(9.0), pvalue=np.float64(0.125))
```

This is similar to the detection of ties, which are also handled in a specific way by the test. However, in the case of ties the current implementation seems to handle numerical precision to some degree (by function [`_rankdata`](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/54ef5423f2e4376230ec3bfda6912a07a50958e3/scipy/stats/_stats_py.py#L10363), I believe):

```py
>>> sp.stats.wilcoxon([10, 20, 30, -10], alternative='greater') # exact tie
WilcoxonResult(statistic=np.float64(8.5), pvalue=np.float64(0.1875))
>>> sp.stats.wilcoxon([10, 20, 30, -10+1e-15], alternative='greater') # approximate tie, fail
WilcoxonResult(statistic=np.float64(9.0), pvalue=np.float64(0.125))
>>> sp.stats.wilcoxon([10, 20, 30, -10+1e-16], alternative='greater') # approximate tie, success
WilcoxonResult(statistic=np.float64(8.5), pvalue=np.float64(0.1875))
```

As shown, the numerical precision threshold for me happens somewhere between 1e-15 and 1e-16. I would expect similar behavior when detecting zeros.

### Reproducing Code Example

```python
import scipy as sp

# zeos
sp.stats.wilcoxon([10, 20, 30, 0], alternative='greater')
sp.stats.wilcoxon([10, 20, 30, 1e-100], alternative='greater')
sp.stats.wilcoxon([10, 20, 30, -1e-100], alternative='greater')

# ties
sp.stats.wilcoxon([10, 20, 30, -10], alternative='greater')
sp.stats.wilcoxon([10, 20, 30, -10+1e-15], alternative='greater')
sp.stats.wilcoxon([10, 20, 30, -10+1e-16], alternative='greater')
```

body:
### Describe your issue.

I have encountered unusual behaviour with `scipy.sparse.linalg.lsqr`. 

I am using the variance reported by LSQR (the estimated diagonals of `(A.T@A)^(-1)`) but the estimated variance is too low. The level that it is too low seems to  depend on the number of data points relative to the number of model parameters. For ~1,000 data points and ~500 model parameters the variance reported by SciPy's implementation of LSQR is low by a factor of 5. 

In the figure below I am computing the diagonals of `(A.T@A)^(-1)` directly and comparing to what `scipy.sparse.linalg.lsqr` returns. If everything was working correctly, I should expect to see this line hover around `y=1`. Less than 1 indicates LSQR is under-estimating the uncertainties. I set extremely strict tolerances for convergence, and it does not appear that `lsqr` is stopping early. For small numbers of parameters, LSQR provides the correct variance estimates. As the number of parameters grows, LSQR underestimates the variance by between a factor of 2x or 5x in these examples. However, as the number of model parameters increases further and gets close to the number of data points, the variance from LSQR becomes closer to the truth.

![che1](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/92042608-37d8-4f85-87f5-569360e42a80)

I plotted the summary statistics returned from LSQR (second figure) but they did not obviously explain the behaviour I see.

![che2](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a1f8b9a7-675f-4434-bfbb-4432e190f472)

I could not find any tests in scipy's implementation that verifies whether the estimated variance is realistic or not.

If anyone knows something about this, I would appreciate your input.

### Reproducing Code Example

```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.sparse import linalg
from scipy.linalg import cho_factor, cho_solve

np.random.seed(0)

fig2, ax_metas = plt.subplots(2, 4)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for n in (250, 501, 1001):

    ms = []
    ratios = []
    metas = []
    pylops_ratios = []
    for m in np.unique(np.logspace(0, np.log10(n), 100).astype(int)):
        if m > n:
            continue
        A = np.random.randn(n, m)
        x_true = np.random.randn(m)
        #noise, var = (0, np.ones(n))
        var = np.random.uniform(0.5, 1.5, n)
        noise = np.random.randn(n) * 0.1
        y = A @ x_true + noise

        C = np.diag(var)
        Cinv = np.diag(1/var)

        # Method 1: Direct solve
        direct_cov = np.linalg.solve(A.T @ Cinv @ A, np.eye(m))
        direct_var = np.diag(direct_cov)    

        # Method 2: LSQR with Cholesky
        L = np.linalg.cholesky(C)
        Linv = np.linalg.inv(L)
        A_white = Linv @ A
        y_white = Linv @ y
        x_chol, *meta, var_chol = linalg.lsqr(A_white, y_white, calc_var=True, show=False, atol=1e-12, btol=1e-12, damp=1e-6, iter_lim=10000000)
        ms.append(m)
        ratios.append(np.mean(var_chol/direct_var))
        metas.append(meta)


    ms = np.array(ms)
    metas = np.array(metas)
    for j, ax_meta in enumerate(ax_metas.flat):
        ax_meta.scatter(ms/n, metas[:, j], label=f"n={n}")

    ax.scatter(ms/n, ratios, label=f"n={n}")

labels = ("istop", "itn", "r1norm", "r2norm", "anorm", "acond", "arnorm", "xnorm")

for j, ax_meta in enumerate(ax_metas.flat):
    ax_meta.set_ylabel(labels[j])
    ax_meta.set_xlabel(f"number of parameters / number of data points")

ax.legend()
ax.set_xlabel(f"number of parameters / number of data points")
ax.set_ylabel(f"mean of [(diagonal from scipy.sparse.linalg.lsqr) / (diagonal from direct solve)]")

fig.suptitle("Computing diagonals of (A.T @ C^(-1) @ A)^(-1) from LSQR")
```

title: MAINT: linalg: consistent output when core dimensions have zero length

labels.name: maintenance

body:
#### Reference issue Closes gh-20372 https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/24148#issuecomment-5462832570 #### What does this implement/fix? Extends `_apply_over_batch` decorator to produce output(s) with the correct shape/dtype when input _core_ dimensions have zero length. #### Additional information There will be a lot of failures in the first CI run. - Some are due to missing `signature` arguments of the `_apply_over_batch` decorator. I ran out of steam and didn't want to write them for `cossin` and `qr`; I think those are the only ones missing now. - Some are due to inconsistency between the output the decorator assumes to be correct and the output that existing tests check for. - Some seem to be real failures due to functions not respecting dtypes. I'll investigate them, fix what I can, and skip/open issues for the rest. One difficulty is that we can't write new, strong, generic tests here. For zero-size _batch_ tests (previous PRs), we determined the expected output dtype and core shape based on the output of a call with non-zero-size input. Here, we can't necssarily do that because the output shape will depend on the shape of the zero-size input, and we can't rely on the function to produce correct output in a call with zero-size input. We could test against the same `signature` information that the decorator uses to produce the output, but this just tests that the decorator is behaving as expected. But that is is already tested extensively, so I'm not sure what we want to do. There are already manually-written tests for a few functions, so maybe those are enough to validate this approach, and exhaustive testing for every function is not needed. #### AI Generation Disclosure ~~No AI~~ After putting this together, I had AI check all the signatures. It found a few real mistakes, so I've fixed them in [b39da12](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/26087/commits/b39da12e694799a215938c566811f67becd4e3d5) and updated tests where possible. The issue with `qr_update` has to do with the function itself; I can't handle it here.
# Zero-size core dimensions in `scipy.linalg`: refined audit This is the second-pass audit of [`linalg_zero_size_output.md`](linalg_zero_size_output.md). It compares the expected mathematical or semantic result with the current source behavior. Private decorated helpers are represented by their public functions. Python and Cython sources/templates are included. The inventory contains 61 public APIs, expanded to 85 signature/variant entries. A signature below is the signature currently declared in the source, unless it is explicitly marked as inferred. ## Potentially nonzero-size cases: current behavior is appropriate
pinvh(..., return_rank=True): (i,j)->(i,j),int() The current result has an empty pseudoinverse and scalar rank `0`, as it should. `pinvh` is square in its documented domain, so the matrix shape is not problematic here.
eigvalsh_tridiagonal(d, e): (i),(j)->(i) The valid case `i=1,j=0` is handled by the implementation and returns the sole diagonal value `d[0]`. Empty zero-by-zero cases return an empty array.
eigh_tridiagonal(..., eigvals_only=True): (i),(j)->(i,) For `i=1,j=0`, the current implementation returns `d[0]`, as expected; for the empty zero-by-zero case it returns an empty eigenvalue array.
eigh_tridiagonal(..., eigvals_only=False): (i),(j)->(i,),(i,i) For `i=1,j=0`, the current implementation returns the sole eigenvalue and a one-by-one eigenvector, equivalent to the identity up to normalization. Empty zero-by-zero inputs return empty factors.
polar(..., side='right'): (i,j)->(i,j),(j,j) For `i=0,j>0`, the current zero-size result has empty `U` and an all-zero `j`-by-`j` `P`, which is the canonical positive-semidefinite factor of the zero matrix.
polar(..., side='left'): (i,j)->(i,j),(i,i) For `j=0,i>0`, the current result has empty `U` and an all-zero `i`-by-`i` `P`, as expected.
qr_multiply(..., pivoting=True, ...): inferred QR/product shapes plus pivot vector The decorator has no explicit signature. For a zero-row input with `j>0`, the current empty-QR path returns an identity permutation of length `j`; the other returned factors are empty. This is a natural and valid pivot result.
qr_delete(..., which='row', N=0, M>p>0, ...): inferred QR-factor shapes For a full QR factorization of an `M`-by-zero matrix, deleting `p` rows should return a nonempty orthogonal `Q1` of shape `(M-p,M-p)` and an empty `R1`. The current source follows this factor-shape logic, so the result is consistent with the expected decomposition.
qr_insert(..., which='row', M=0, N>0, p>0, ...): inferred QR-factor shapes Inserting `p` rows into the full factors of a zero-row, `N`-column matrix should produce `Q1` with shape `(p,p)` and `R1` with shape `(p,N)`. The current source constructs those factors, including the identity-like new orthogonal block, so this case is appropriate.
qr_insert(..., which='col', M>0, N=0, p>0, ...): inferred QR-factor shapes Inserting `p` columns into the full factors of an `M`-row, zero-column matrix should produce nonempty updated factors when `M,p>0`. The current source supports this shape transition, so the result is consistent with the expected decomposition.
rq(..., mode='full', ...): (i,j)->(i,j),(j,j) For `i=0,j>0`, the current empty-array path returns empty `R` and `Q=eye(j)`. That is a valid full RQ decomposition of the empty matrix.
schur(..., sort=...,): (i,i)->(i,i),(i,i),() For an empty matrix with sorting requested, the current result contains empty `T` and `Z` and scalar `sdim=0`, which is correct.
null_space(A): (m,n)->(n,n) For `A.shape==(0,n)`, the whole `n`-dimensional domain is the null space. The current SVD path returns an orthonormal basis of that space, conventionally the identity. For `n=0`, it returns an empty basis.
subspace_angles(...): (i,j),(i,k)->float(min(j,k),) For `i=0,j,k>0`, the requested positive number of principal angles is undefined because both column spaces collapse to the zero subspace. The current result is a NaN array of shape `(min(j,k),)`, which is an appropriate way to preserve the declared output shape without inventing angles.
expm_cond(A): (i,i)->float() The empty case reduces the relative condition-number expression to zero over zero. The current result is `NaN`, which correctly reports that the condition number is undefined.
orthogonal_procrustes(A, B): (i,j),(i,j)->(j,j),float() If either `i=0` or `j=0`, the current implementation returns an orthogonal `R` factor (the identity in the empty-data case) and `scale=0`. The objective contains no data, so any orthogonal `R` is optimal; identity is a valid canonical choice.
leslie(f, s): (i),(j)->(i,i) The signature permits the one-age case `i=1,j=0`, which would naturally give `[[f[0]]]`. The current implementation rejects `s` of length zero. This is consistent with the documented precondition that `s` must have length at least one; supporting one age class would be a separate API decision.
convolution_matrix(..., mode='full'): (m)->(m+n-1,n) For `m=0`, the signature can describe a nonzero output, but the documented contract requires a nonempty kernel. The current implementation raises a `ValueError`, which is preferable to fabricating a convolution matrix.
convolution_matrix(..., mode='same'): (m)->(m if m>n else n,n) The current implementation likewise rejects `m=0`, as required by its nonempty-kernel precondition.
convolution_matrix(..., mode='valid'): (m)->(m-n+1 if m>n else n-m+1,n) The current implementation rejects `m=0`, which is the appropriate behavior under the documented contract.
solveh_banded(..., ...): (i,j),(j)->(j) For `i=0,j>0`, the current default empty-core path returns a NaN vector. A zero-row band storage has no main diagonal and cannot define a positive- definite banded system. NaNs appropriately mark the solution as undefined.
solveh_banded(..., ...): (i,j),(j,k)->(j,k) For `i=0,j,k>0`, the current result is a NaN matrix. The input has no valid positive-definite banded system, so NaNs appropriately mark the result as undefined.
eig_banded(..., eigvals_only=False): (i,j)->float(j,),(j,j) For `i=0,j>0`, the current path returns NaN eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the declared shapes. Empty band storage has no defined eigenproblem, so NaNs are an appropriate result.
eig_banded(..., eigvals_only=True): (i,j)->float(j,) The current result is a NaN vector for `i=0,j>0`. It should instead reject the zero-band representation only if the API chooses strict validation; under the current undefined-value convention, the NaN result is appropriate.
eigvals_banded(...): (i,j)->float(j,) The current result is a NaN vector when the band-count dimension is zero. No eigenvalues are defined by an empty band representation, so NaNs are appropriate.
cho_solve_banded(..., b vector): (i,j),(j)->(j) For `i=0,j>0`, the current result is a NaN solution vector. A Cholesky banded factor must contain at least the main diagonal; NaNs appropriately represent the undefined solution.
cho_solve_banded(..., b matrix): (i,j),(j,k)->(j,k) For `i=0,j,k>0`, the current result is a NaN solution matrix. The factor is structurally invalid, so NaNs appropriately represent the undefined result.
## Potentially nonzero-size cases: current behavior does not match the expected result
pinv(..., return_rank=True): (i,j)->(i,j),int() The scalar rank is correctly `0`, but for a nonsquare zero-size input the pseudoinverse should have shape `(j,i)`, not `(i,j)`. The current declared signature and zero-core result preserve the wrong matrix orientation.
clarkson_woodruff_transform(input_matrix, ...): (i,j)->(k,j) For an input of shape `(0,j)` with `k,j>0`, the transform is multiplication by a `k`-by-zero sketch matrix, so the correct result is an all-zero `(k,j)` matrix. The current public path tries to construct the random sketch with a zero input-row range and raises before producing that result.
issymmetric(a): (i,i)->bool() An empty square matrix is symmetric by convention, so the scalar result should be `True`. The current decorator instead fills the Boolean scalar with `False` before the function can apply that convention.
ishermitian(a): (i,i)->bool() An empty square matrix is Hermitian by convention, so the scalar result should be `True`. The current decorator instead fills the Boolean scalar with `False`, which does not match the documented convention.
qr_update(..., u.shape=(M,0), v.shape=(N,0), ...): inferred Q/R shapes A rank-zero update should be a no-op and return the original nonempty `Q,R`. The current source reaches the update kernels without a dedicated rank-zero case; in particular, its special `M=1` path combines nonempty `R` with empty update vectors. It therefore does not reliably implement the expected no-op.
## Always-zero-size cases: current behavior is appropriate
solve_triangular(..., b vector): (i,i),(i)->(i) Zero-size compatible systems produce an empty solution vector. The current result has the correct zero size.
solve_triangular(..., b matrix): (i,i),(i,j)->(i,j) If `i=0` or `j=0`, the solution is empty. The current result is appropriate.
solve_banded(..., b vector): (i),(j),(l+u+1,m),(m)->(m) Valid zero-size systems have `m=0`, so the solution is empty. The current result is appropriate; `l+u+1` cannot be zero for valid `l,u`.
solve_banded(..., b matrix): (i),(j),(l+u+1,m),(m,n)->(m,n) For `m=0` or `n=0`, the solution has zero size. The current result is appropriate.
solve_toeplitz(..., b vector): (i),(i),(i)->(i) Any zero core dimension forces an empty solution. The current result is appropriate.
solve_toeplitz(..., b matrix): (i),(i),(i,j)->(i,j) If `i=0` or `j=0`, the solution is empty. The current result is appropriate.
pinvh(..., return_rank=False): (i,j)->(i,j) The square pseudoinverse is empty for a zero-size input. The current result is appropriate.
matrix_balance(..., separate=False): (i,i)->(i,i),(i,i) Both balanced matrix outputs are empty for `i=0`. The current result is appropriate.
matrix_balance(..., separate=True): (i,i)->(i,i),(2,i) For `i=0`, the balanced matrix and the `(2,0)` permutation/scale data are empty. The current result is appropriate.
hessenberg(..., calc_q=False): (i,i)->(i,i) The empty Hessenberg matrix is the correct result, and the current result is empty.
hessenberg(..., calc_q=True): (i,i)->(i,i),(i,i) Both empty square outputs are correct for `i=0`.
cho_solve(..., b vector): (i,i),(i)->(i) The zero-size solution vector is empty, as is the current result.
cho_solve(..., b matrix): (i,i),(i,j)->(i,j) The solution is empty when `i=0` or `j=0`; the current result is appropriate.
ldl(A): (i,i)->(i,i),(i,i),int(i) The empty `L`, `D`, and permutation vector are correct for `i=0`; the current result is appropriate.
lu_factor(a): (i,j)->(i,j),int(min(i,j)) The factor and pivot vector are empty when either matrix dimension is zero. The current result is appropriate.
lu_solve(..., b vector): (i,i),(i),(i)->(i) The zero-size solution vector is empty, as expected.
lu_solve(..., b matrix): (i,i),(i),(i,j)->(i,j) The solution is empty when `i=0` or `j=0`, as is the current result.
qr_multiply(..., pivoting=False, ...): inferred QR/product shapes without pivots With no pivot output, compatible zero-size products and `R` factors are empty. The current empty-array path is appropriate.
rq(..., mode='economic', ...): (i,j)->(i,k),(k,j), k=min(i,j) If either `i=0` or `j=0`, `k=0` and both factors are empty. The current implementation returns these shapes.
rq(..., mode='r', ...): (i,j)->(i,j) The `R` factor is empty for either zero matrix dimension. The current result is appropriate.
qz(A, B): (i,i),(i,i)->(i,i),(i,i),(i,i),(i,i) All four empty square factors are appropriate for `i=0`.
ordqz(A, B): (i,i),(i,i)->(i,i),(i,i),complex(i),(i),(i,i),(i,i) All matrix and length-`i` outputs are empty when `i=0`. The current result is appropriate.
schur(..., sort=None): (i,i)->(i,i),(i,i) The current empty `T` and `Z` are the correct results.
rsf2csf(T, Z): (i,i),(i,i)->complex(i,i),complex(i,i) Both converted factors are empty for `i=0`, as expected.
diagsvd(s, ..., ...): (i)->(M,N) For valid zero-length `s`, either `M=0` or `N=0`; the output matrix is empty. The current result is appropriate.
cholesky_banded(ab): (i,j)->(i,j) For valid empty banded matrices, the output is empty and the current result is appropriate. A zero band-count dimension with `j>0` is structurally invalid and should be rejected rather than silently accepted; this is a validation gap, not a nonzero-output case.
cossin(...): inferred CS-decomposition block shapes No explicit NEP 5 signature is declared. The public whole-matrix interface rejects zero partitions (`p` and `q` must be positive); the block interface does not promise a zero-row partition. For documented valid empty cases there is no nonzero output to construct, and the current behavior is not a defined public zero-size contract.
expm_frechet(A, E, compute_expm=True): (i,i),(i,i)->(i,i),(i,i) The empty exponential and empty Frechet derivative are correct.
expm_frechet(A, E, compute_expm=False): (i,i),(i,i)->(i,i) The empty derivative matrix is correct.
fractional_matrix_power(A, ...): (i,i)->complex(i,i) The empty square matrix is the correct result, and the current result is empty.
logm(A): (i,i)->(i,i) The current result for `i=0` is the unique empty matrix, as expected.
cosm(A): (i,i)->(i,i) The empty matrix is the correct zero-size result.
sinm(A): (i,i)->(i,i) The empty matrix is the correct zero-size result.
tanm(A): (i,i)->(i,i) The empty matrix is the correct zero-size result.
coshm(A): (i,i)->(i,i) The empty matrix is the correct zero-size result.
sinhm(A): (i,i)->(i,i) The empty matrix is the correct zero-size result.
tanhm(A): (i,i)->(i,i) The empty matrix is the correct zero-size result.
funm(A, ...): (i,i)->(i,i) The empty matrix is the correct zero-size result.
signm(A): (i,i)->(i,i) The empty matrix is the correct zero-size result.
khatri_rao(a, b): (i,k),(j,k)->(i*j,k) Any zero core dimension makes the output empty. The current result is appropriate.
solve_sylvester(a, b, q): (i,i),(j,j),(i,j)->(i,j) If `i=0` or `j=0`, the solution is empty. The current result is appropriate.
solve_continuous_lyapunov(a, q): (i,i),(i,i)->(i,i) The empty square solution is correct and is what the current code returns.
solve_discrete_lyapunov(a, q): (i,i),(i,i)->(i,i) The empty square solution is correct and is what the current code returns.
solve_continuous_are(a, b, q, r, e, s): (i,i),...,(i,i)->(i,i) The Riccati solution is empty when `i=0`; the current batching result is appropriate.
solve_discrete_are(a, b, q, r, e, s): (i,i),...,(i,i)->(i,i) The Riccati solution is empty when `i=0`; the current batching result is appropriate.
toeplitz(c, r): (i),(j)->(i,j) If either vector is empty, the matrix has a zero row or column dimension. The current result is empty, as expected.
hankel(c, r): (i),(j)->(i,j) If either vector is empty, the Hankel matrix is empty. The current result is appropriate.
fiedler_companion(a): (i)->(i-1,i-1) For fewer than two coefficients, the documented result is empty. The current implementation returns an empty one-dimensional array for `i=0` and an empty `(0,0)` matrix for `i=1`; this is semantically empty, although the written arithmetic signature needs a conditional form for `i<2`.
## Always-zero-size cases: current behavior does not match the expected result
pinv(..., return_rank=False): (i,j)->(i,j) The pseudoinverse should have shape `(j,i)`. The current zero-core result uses the declared `(i,j)` shape, which is wrong for nonsquare inputs even though both arrays have zero size.
matmul_toeplitz(...): (i),(j),(j)->(i) The declared signature is inconsistent with the public argument ordering and the implementation: `x` is validated against the first (row) vector, while the output length is determined by the second (column) vector. A valid empty column vector with a nonempty row vector should produce an empty result, but the current decorator can reject it because it applies the mismatched signature. The signature should instead describe `(i),(j),(i)->(j)`.
matmul_toeplitz(...): (i),(j),(j,k)->(i,k) The same argument-order mismatch affects matrix right-hand sides. The signature should be `(i),(j),(i,k)->(j,k)` for the decorated helper, so valid zero-size products are accepted and returned with the correct shape.
orth(A): (i,j)->(i,j) For `A.shape==(0,j)`, the mathematical range has rank zero and the result should have shape `(0,0)`, not merely the declared empty shape `(0,j)`. The current default zero-core result has shape `(0,j)`. It has zero size, but the shape is not the documented `(M,K)` range-basis shape.
cholesky_banded(ab): (i,j)->(i,j) When `i=0,j>0`, the current decorator returns an empty array instead of rejecting a banded representation with no main diagonal. The zero-size shape itself is harmless, but silently accepting this structurally invalid input is not the right validation behavior.

title: BUG: sparse.linalg.LinearOperator: missing state when unpickling in v1.18.0

labels.name: defect
labels.description: A clear bug or issue that prevents SciPy from being installed or used as expected

labels.name: backport-candidate
labels.description: This fix should be ported by a maintainer to previous SciPy versions.

body:
### Describe your issue.

`scipy.sparse.linalg.LinearOperator.__getstate__` (new in scipy 1.18.0) drops all `__slots__`-declared attributes when pickling a `LinearOperator` subclass, silently. No exception is raised at pickle time — the state is simply missing after unpickling — so the failure only surfaces later, wherever the first dropped attribute happens to be accessed. In a real program, that can be arbitrarily far from the pickle call site (e.g. inside a `multiprocessing`/`concurrent.futures` worker process), which makes this very difficult to diagnose from the resulting traceback alone.

### Root cause

`LinearOperator.__getstate__` was added in 1.18.0, apparently to make the new Array API namespace reference (`_xp`) picklable:

```python
# scipy/sparse/linalg/_interface.py
def __getstate__(self):
    state = self.__dict__.copy()
    state["_xp"] = state["_xp"].empty(0)
    return state
```
This returns only `self.__dict__`. It has no knowledge of `__slots__`.

Before 1.18.0, `LinearOperator` defined no `__getstate__`/`__reduce__` at all, so pickling fell back to Python's default, slot-aware mechanism, which correctly serializes both `__dict__` *and* every `__slots__` attribute declared anywhere in the instance's class MRO.

Because `LinearOperator.__getstate__` now overrides that default for every subclass, any `LinearOperator` subclass that stores its state in `__slots__` — a common, memory-conscious pattern for `LinearOperator`
subclasses — silently loses that state on every pickle/unpickle round-trip.

### Reproducing Code Example

```python
import pickle
import numpy as np
from scipy.sparse.linalg import LinearOperator


class DiagonalOperator(LinearOperator):
    """A minimal LinearOperator subclass storing its state in __slots__."""

    __slots__ = ["_diagonal"]

    def __init__(self, diagonal):
        self._diagonal = np.asarray(diagonal, dtype=np.float64)
        super().__init__(dtype=self._diagonal.dtype, shape=(len(diagonal),) * 2)

    def _matvec(self, x):
        return self._diagonal * x


op = DiagonalOperator([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
print(hasattr(op, "_diagonal"))       # True

op2 = pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(op))
print(hasattr(op2, "_diagonal"))      # False on >=1.18.0, True on <1.18.0

op2.matvec(np.ones(3))                # AttributeError on >=1.18.0
```

### Error message

```shell

  File "repro_linearoperator_slots_pickle.py", line 70, in <module>
    main()
  File "repro_linearoperator_slots_pickle.py", line 66, in main
    print("matvec after pickle:", op2.matvec(np.ones(3)))
                                   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File ".../scipy/sparse/linalg/_interface.py", line 391, in matvec
    return self._shared_matvec(x)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File ".../scipy/sparse/linalg/_interface.py", line 353, in _shared_matvec
    y = self._rmatvec(x) if adjoint else self._matvec(x)
                                         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "repro_linearoperator_slots_pickle.py", line 50, in _matvec
    return self._diagonal * x
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
AttributeError: 'DiagonalOperator' object has no attribute '_diagonal'
```

title: BUG: linalg: prevent a segfault in `inv(f_order_sym_matrix, overwrite_a=True)`

labels.name: defect

body:
#### Reference issue
<!--Example: Closes gh-WXYZ.-->

closes gh-26045


#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

`linalg.inv` does several optimizations internally, and two of them conspired to a segfault:
- for symmetric inputs, it first tries a Cholesky-based invert; if that fails (i.e. the input is symmetric but not positive definite), it falls back to the symmetric invese;
- for `overwrite_a`, it works in-place to save memory

Thus, for a symmetric input in the memory-saving mode, what happened was:

- we try `?potrf` in-place, and it overwrites the input matrix;
- if it failed, we need to restore the original input, but it's been destroyed already.

Therefore, in this PR we go straight to the symmetric inverse if `overwrite_a=True`.

#### Reference issue
<!--Example: Closes gh-WXYZ.-->
Closes gh-24681.

#### What does this implement/fix?
`_fir_mirror_symmetric` handles an out-of-bounds index only once, so it requires
`2*(len(filt)//2)` samples along the axis being filtered. On a shorter axis it read
past both ends of the input, and once `len(filt)//2` grew larger than the axis size
it also wrote outside the output; the values returned were whatever was stored in
the adjacent heap space. Validate both axes in `FIRsepsym2d` instead of relying on
the caller.

The bound is exact, not the `len(filt) <= n` the TODO suggests, where `n` is the
length of the filtered axis: `len(filt) == n + 1` is still in-bounds and matches a
mirror-symmetric reference convolution, so it stays accepted.

This also removes the ASAN suppression and the two xfail markers that were hiding
the problem. `test_sepfir2d_strided_2` only ever called `sepfir2d` with a filter
too long for its image, so it is replaced by `test_sepfir2d_filter_too_long`;
`test_sepfir2d_strided_3` keeps its valid half, and its expected dtype is now
pinned, which the xfail had been masking as well.

#### Additional information
<!--Any additional information you think is important.-->
The bound was checked four independent ways, all agreeing on
`N >= 2*(len(filt)//2)`:

| check | result |
|---|---|
| index-range sweep over `(N, len(filt))` | 54/54 agree; also shows the output overflow |
| ASAN on a verbatim copy of the function | 50/50 agree; clean at the boundary |
| all-ones 4x4 image, `len(filt) == 7` | correct answer 225; got `min=145`, and `min=17` on a rerun |
| vs. a mirror-symmetric reference convolution | identical for every in-bounds `(N, len(filt))` |

Because the results for the rejected inputs were undefined, there is no output any
caller could have relied on; the same call returned different values on reruns.

`scipy/signal/tests/test_bsplines.py` goes from 24 passed / 5 xfailed / 2 xpassed
to 39 passed with no xfails. Full `scipy.signal`: 15916 passed, 4 skipped, 0 failed.

title: TST: loosen signal test tolerances for FMA-contraction builds

labels.name: maintenance
labels.description: Items related to regular maintenance tasks

labels.name: backport-candidate
labels.description: This fix should be ported by a maintainer to previous SciPy versions.

body:
This handles the test-tolerance side of #25488. A few signal tests fail when SciPy is built with certain fast-math CPU settings that change how the math rounds in the last few digits. The results aren't wrong, just slightly different, but a few tests are strict enough to flag the tiny gap. The fix is to loosen those tolerances, as suggested in the issue.

Three changes:

- test_nyquist: raised the allowed error for the 32-bit-float case. It failed just over the old limit, and the issue notes it also fails on some ARM machines, so I left room for both.

- test_roundtrip_float32: a looser limit already existed here but only ran on one old chip type. The issue isn't tied to that chip (it shows up on ARM and fast-math builds too), so I applied the looser limit to all 32-bit-float cases and dropped a now-unused import.

- test_roundtrip_scaling: different case. A percentage margin was suggested, but it checks against exact zero, and a percentage of zero is still zero. So it needed a small fixed margin instead, matching what the test already does a few lines below.

I can't build with these settings locally, so it'd be good to confirm they pass on a znver5/skylake build before merging.

The two linprog failures aren't covered here. Those fail earlier, in the solver itself, before any tolerance check, so they're a separate problem. Can open a separate issue if useful.

title: ENH: stats: Add distance correlation, distance covariance, and energy distance (#13728)

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: A new feature or improvement

body:
#### Reference issue
Closes #13728

#### What does this implement/fix?
This PR implements **multivariate distance correlation**, **distance covariance**, and **energy distance** in `scipy.stats._distance_correlation`, completely derived from primary literature (Székely et al., 2007; Székely & Rizzo, 2014; Rizzo & Székely, 2016).

Unlike external packages (e.g. `hyppo` or `dcor`), this implementation is **100% pure Python/NumPy/SciPy**, completely free of third-party compilation dependencies (no Numba required), and fully compliant with SciPy's BSD-3 licensing.

#### Key Functions Added:
1. **`distance_covariance(x, y, *, method="auto", metric="euclidean")`**:
   - Computes sample distance covariance $d\text{Cov}_n(X, Y)$ using $O(n^2)$ vectorized double-centering.
   - Non-negative for all samples; equals 0 if and only if $X$ and $Y$ are independent.
   - Supports classical biased estimation and unbiased U-centering estimator (Székely & Rizzo, 2014).
2. **`distance_correlation(x, y, *, method="auto", metric="euclidean")`**:
   - Scale- and dimension-free dependence metric $d\text{Cor}_n(X, Y) \in [0, 1]$.
   - Sensitive to arbitrary non-linear associations (circular, parabolic, sinusoidal, cluster) where Pearson correlation is 0.
3. **`distance_covariance_test(x, y, *, permutations=999, metric="euclidean", workers=1, random_state=None)`**:
   - Nonparametric permutation test of independence returning `DistanceCovarianceResult(statistic, pvalue, null_distribution)`.
   - Optimized permutation engine: pre-computes double-centered distance matrices once; evaluates row-and-column indexed permutations $B_{\pi} = B[\pi, :][:, \pi]$ in $O(n^2)$ without recomputing distances or means.
   - Supports multi-processing via `MapWrapper`.
4. **`energy_distance_nd(u, v, *, metric="euclidean")`**:
   - Multivariate energy distance test statistic for equality of distributions in arbitrary dimensions $\mathbb{R}^d$.

#### Unit Tests:
- Added `scipy/stats/tests/test_distance_correlation.py` with 29 comprehensive unit tests (100% passing) covering input validation, mathematical symmetries, linear invariance, non-linear dependence detection, permutation calibration, and distribution shift detection.

title: DOC: special: improve Mathieu functions documentation

labels.name: Documentation
labels.description: Issues related to the SciPy documentation. Also check https://github.com/scipy/scipy.org

labels.name: C/C++
labels.description: Items related to the internal C/C++ code base

body:
#### Reference issue [Discussion](https://discuss.scientific-python.org/t/proposal-switch-the-mathieu-functions-to-radians-for-scipy-2-0/2560/3) from @steppi and @brorson #### What does this implement/fix? This PR tries to improve the various inconsistencies found in the documentation of Mathieu functions, the most important being that the derivatives of `mathieu_cem` and `mathieu_sem` are per radian, while the angular argument `x` is in degrees (I found this to be very confusing btw). Also, the modified Mathieu functions' argument is (as far as I can tell) dimensionless, while the current doc says it is in degrees. #### Additional information The following Python script highlights the confusion. It corresponds to the case m=1, q=0, for which `mathieu_cem` boils down to the `cos` function.
```python import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np from scipy.special import mathieu_cem m = 1 q = 0 xs = np.linspace(0, 360, 1000) y, yp = mathieu_cem(m, q, xs) # Because xs is measured in degrees, this is dy/d(x in degrees). yp_numerical = np.gradient(y, xs) # SciPy returns dy/d(theta), where theta is the angle in radians. # Convert it to a derivative per degree. yp_per_degree = yp * np.pi / 180 fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots( 2, 1, figsize=(8, 7), sharex=True, constrained_layout=True ) ax1.plot(xs, y, label=r"$\mathrm{ce}_1(x, 0)$") ax1.plot(xs, np.cos(np.radians(xs)), "--", label=r"$\cos(x)$") ax1.set_ylabel("y") ax1.set_title("Mathieu function and derivative unit mismatch") ax1.grid() ax1.legend() ax2.plot( xs, yp, label="Returned derivative (per radian)", linewidth=2, ) ax2.plot( xs, yp_numerical, "--", label="Numerical derivative w.r.t. degrees", ) ax2.plot( xs, yp_per_degree, ":", linewidth=3, label=r"Returned derivative $\times\,\pi/180$", ) ax2.set_xlabel("x (degrees)") ax2.set_ylabel("derivative") ax2.grid() ax2.legend() plt.show() ```
#### AI Generation Disclosure I first drafted the Python script while reviewing the Mathieu documentation and worked on improving the doc. I then asked Codex for a review and feedback, and worked with it to finish the PR.

labels.name: maintenance

body:
Towards gh-3432.

gh-3432 asks for better test coverage of `scipy.signal.windows`. Rather than
guess which windows look under-tested, I measured it: running the existing
`scipy/signal/tests/test_windows.py` under `coverage --branch` puts
`scipy/signal/windows/_windows.py` at 99% with exactly two uncovered statements
and two uncovered branches, both in `dpss`:

- `if norm not in known_norms: raise ValueError(...)` — an invalid `norm`
  argument is never passed.
- `if singleton: ratios = ratios[0]` — `return_ratios=True` is never combined
  with `Kmax=None`.

The second is a behaviour worth pinning rather than just a line: with
`Kmax=None`, `dpss` drops the leading axis, so the returned ratio is 0-d instead
of shape `(1,)`, and nothing asserts that today.
`test_degenerate_single_samples` does call `dpss(1, 1., return_ratios=True)`,
but `M=1` returns early through `_len_guards` and never reaches the line.

This PR adds tests only, no source changes:

- `TestDPSS.test_ratios_kmax_none` checks the `Kmax=None` shape contract and
  that the window and ratio agree with the explicit `Kmax=1` case. Since
  `Kmax=None` defaults to `norm='approximate'` and `Kmax=1` defaults to
  `norm=2`, the comparison requests `norm='approximate'` explicitly.
- two `assert_raises` lines in the existing `TestDPSS.test_degenerate` for an
  unknown `norm` (a string and an int).

With these, `scipy/signal/windows/_windows.py` reaches 100% line and branch
coverage under that test file.

One disclosure: the coverage figures above were measured against an installed
scipy 1.17.1 rather than a local `dev.py` build, so please treat the exact
line numbers as indicative.

Happy to fold the `norm` checks into a parametrized test or move the new test
elsewhere in `TestDPSS` if you prefer a different layout.

### AI Declaration
As per SciPy's AI Policy, I disclose that ChatGPT was used as an assistant to check branch coverage details for `scipy.signal.windows.dpss` and to assist in formatting the unit test snippets (`test_ratios_kmax_none` and boundary checking assertions in `test_degenerate`). labels.name: maintenance

body:
#### Reference issue
Toward gh-25964

#### What does this implement/fix?
Previously, `linalg.eig` maintained a dtype instability for backward compatibility: the output dtype of the eigenvectors - but not the eigenvalues - would be forced to real dtype if all imaginary components were zero.

This PR eliminates the shim to make the output dtype of `scipy.linalg.eig` consistent with `numpy.linalg.eig` and the array API standard. Besides making the behavior predictable for users, this facilitates dtype testing of `eig` in special cases (e.g. zero-size input).

#### Additional information
This was discussed in the context of NumPy in https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/29000 and the change was implemented in https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/30411.

This suggests an immediate change rather than `FutureWarning` cycle because users would not be able to silence the warning by changing their input. We are coming up to a major version increment, so this is the best time for such a change.

[Forum post](https://discuss.scientific-python.org/t/fixing-linalg-eig-dtype-instability/2635) made 9/18/2026.

title: DOC: fix parameter name/type separator in public docstrings

labels.name: Documentation

body:
#### Reference issue

None, found while scanning docstrings with `numpydoc`.

#### What does this implement/fix?

numpydoc needs a space before the colon in a parameter line. Where it is missing, the whole `name: type` string is parsed as the parameter name and the type is dropped, so the rendered page shows a plain line instead of a name with its type. On the published [`ShortTimeFFT.from_window`](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.signal.ShortTimeFFT.from_window.html) page, `fs` renders with its `float` type while `win_param: Union[str, tuple, float],` renders as one unstyled string.

This fixes the 10 occurrences that affect public pages, in `ShortTimeFFT.from_window`, `OddsRatioResult.confidence_interval`, `multivariate_normal.fit`, `dirichlet_multinomial.logpmf` / `.pmf`, and the `multinomial_frozen` class docstring.

#### Additional information

I found these with an AST walk over the SciPy sources that parses every public docstring with `numpydoc.docscrape.NumpyDocString` and reports parameter names containing a colon. Those three files report 10 such parameters before this change and none after. The remaining matches in the tree are in private helpers or vendored `_external` code, so they do not reach the rendered docs and I left them alone.

One line goes slightly beyond adding a space: `win_param: Union[str, tuple, float],` also had a trailing comma, and I wrote the type as `str | tuple | float` to match `mfft : int | None` a few lines below. Text and defaults are otherwise untouched.

title: RFC: linalg: array api support for `scipy.linalg` functions which are more fully featured versions of functions in the array API linear algebra extensoin

labels.name: RFC
labels.description: Request for Comments; typically used to gather feedback for a substantial change proposal

labels.name: array types
labels.description: Items related to array API support and input array validation (see gh-18286)

body:
`scipy.linalg` has a number of functions that have corresponding functions in the Python array API standard's [Linear Algebra Extension](https://data-apis.org/array-api/2022.12/extensions/linear_algebra_functions.html). The `scipy.linalg` functions provide additional features that go beyond what is in the standard. What should be done about array API support for these `scipy.linalg` functions? There are two possibilities that sound reasonable to me.

##### Plan 1
Mark the `scipy.linalg` functions as out of scope for array API support. To provide array API support for SciPy functions which depend on functionality from the `scipy.linalg` functions that goes beyond what is av ailable in `xp.linalg`, branch on `is_numpy(xp)` and maintain custom codepaths for the non-NumPy case. One idea here is that it may be easier to come up with workarounds for features missing from `xp.linalg` by exploiting the specific structure of problems. 


##### Plan 2
Add array API support for the `scipy.linalg` functions to the best extent that is feasible. Document which features are and aren't supported on which backends. It may be possible to expand the available features on a piecemeal basis.

It may be desirable to select different plans for different functions. There is a fair amount of information below. It's not necessarily intended to be read in one sitting. I'm just laying it out below to have it all in one place for reference purposes.

#### Brief survey of backend availability

Only CuPy and JAX have `scipy.linalg` namespaces. CuPy omits `scipy.linalg` functions from  `cupyx.scipy.linalg` if there is a corresponding version in `cupy.linalg`. `jax.scipy.linalg` has versions of these functions which maintain surface level API compatibility with `scipy.linalg`, but almost without exception all features which go beyond what is in `jax.numpy.linalg` are not supported. Although PyTorch has only `torch.linalg`, in some cases, its versions of these functions go beyond the standard and have additional features. Some features which are not available in alternative backends could perhaps be supported through wrappers that enable them. I'll go into more detail on such things below, but first for reference purposes, here is a list of the functions in question.

#### List of functions

* [scipy.linalg.cholesky](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.linalg.cholesky.html#scipy.linalg.cholesky)(a[,lower, overwrite_a, check_finite]) verse [xp.linalg.cholesky](https://data-apis.org/array-api/latest/extensions/generated/array_api.linalg.cholesky.html#array_api.linalg.cholesky)(x, /)
* [scipy.linalg.det](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.linalg.det.html#scipy.linalg.det)(a[,overwrite_a, check_finite]) verse [xp.linalg.det](https://data-apis.org/array-api/latest/extensions/generated/array_api.linalg.det.html#array_api.linalg.det)(x, /)
* [scipy.linalg.eigh](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.linalg.eigh.html#scipy.linalg.eigh)(a[, b, lower, eigvals_only, ...]) verse [xp.linalg.eigh](https://data-apis.org/array-api/latest/extensions/generated/array_api.linalg.eigh.html#array_api.linalg.eigh)(x, /)

has been merged to add them to the next revision.


* [scipy.linalg.eig](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.linalg.eig.html#scipy.linalg.eig)(a[, b, overwrite_a, check_finite, ...])

The following function is not currently in the linear algebra extension, but is likely to be added in a future version per the latest discussion in https://github.com/data-apis/array-api/pull/240.

* [scipy.linalg.lstsq](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.linalg.lstsq.html#scipy.linalg.lstsq)(a, b[, cond, overwrite_a, ...])


#### Survey of additional features

I may have missed some of the additional features, but think I think at least most fall into the categories below. This is the result of my investigations into what features are available, what other backends if any also of them, and where if anywhere they are used internally in SciPy.


##### `check_finite`

Each of the SciPy versions of these functions have a kwarg `check_finite` which defaults to `check_finite=True`. It enables input validation that checks if all input arrays have only finite values, raising if this is not the case.  None of the alternative backends have `linalg` functions supporting such input validation.`jax.scipy.linalg` versions of these functions have the `check_finite` kwarg but it is ignored because such input validation is incompatible with JAX's JIT compilation. `check_finite` could in principle be supported in these `scipy.linalg` functions for all eager backends.

##### `overwrite_x`

Many of the functions have kwargs like `overwrite_a` and `overwrite_b` for telling the underlying LAPACK implementation it is free but not required to overwrite the input array for the sake of performance gains. None of the alternative backends offer working versions of `these overwrite options`. `jax.scipy.linalg` functions have the kwargs but they are ignored. There is no harm in ignoring these kwargs.

##### Rank revealing QR decomposition

`scipy.linalg.qr` has a kwarg `pivoting` defaulting to `pivoting=False`. When `pivoting=True` a rank-revealing QR decomposition is computed. In the process of computing the decomposition, a column permutation matrix $P$ is computed so that one ends up with the decomposition $AP = QR$ where the pivots in P are chosen so that upper blocks of R will be larger in norm and the lower blocks smaller. If the $k\times k$ lower right block in $R$ is numerically small but the lower $k \times k$ block is not, then $A$ is revealed to be of numerical rank $n - k$, i.e. it is numerically close to being a rank $n - k$ matrix. `jax.scipy.linalg.qr` has the pivoting option and it works on the GPU. `pivoting=True` is used in SciPy in `scipy.optimize.lsq_linear` for solving least squares problems with bounded coefficients, in the `method='trf'` codepath. `lsq_linear` seems like it could in principle be array agnostic.

##### `mode` of QR decomposition

The mode kwarg of `scipy.linalg.qr` takes values `mode="full"`: for returning the full matrices for both $Q$ and $R$,  `mode="r"`: for returning just $R$,  `mode="economic"`: for returning $Q$ and $R$ with shapes $(M, K$$ and $(K, N)$ instead of $(M, M) and $(M, N)$ with `K=min(M, N)`, and `mode="raw"` for returning matrices $Q$ and $\Tau$ in the internal format used by LAPACK. `xp.linalg.qr` has the `mode` kwarg but it only takes values `mode="full"` and `mode="reduced"` where `"reduced"` means the same thing as `"economic"`. PyTorch, CuPy, and JAX each support the `mode="r"` option. `mode="raw"` is not used internally in SciPy,
so there's no harm in this not being supported.

##### Generalized eigenvalue problems

`scipy.linalg.eig`, `scipy.lialg.eigvals`, `scipy.linalg.eigh`, and `scipy.linalg.eighvals` each have an optional argument `b` for solving the [generalized eigenvalue problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigendecomposition_of_a_matrix#Generalized_eigenvalue_problem) $Av = \lambda B v$. None of the alternative backends are able to solve the generalized eigenvalue problem. The JAX versions of these functions in`jax.scipy.linalg` have the `b` arg for surface level API compatability but only `b=None` is supported. The `b` arg is not used much in SciPy outside of tests and benchmarks. The `b` arg of `eigh` is  used in the dense codepath of [`scipy.sparse.linalg.lobpcg`](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.sparse.linalg.lobpcg.html). When `b` is well-conditioned, it's fairly straightforward to reduce to a standard eigenvalue problem with one decomposition or other. For `eigh` one can use the cholesky decomposition. To handle ill-conditioned and singular `b`, one needs the `qz` decomposition, which is notoriously difficult to accelerate with GPUs, and is not available on any of the alternative backends. I'm not sure if it would make sense to support the `b` option for well-conditioned `b`, and document that it won't work for general `b`, but it's doable.

##### `assume_a` for `scipy.linalg.solve` and `scipy.linalg.inv`.

`scipy.linalg.solve` and `scipy.linalg.inv` each has an option `assume_a` for specifying the structure of the matrix $A$. It supports many options. `jax.scipy.linalg.solve` has this option as well and supports a subset of the options. `jax.scipy.linalg.inv` does not have `assume_a` yet. `assume_a` was only added to `scipy.linalg.inv` in 1.17, so I assume it will find it's way into JAX eventually. Although none of the other backends have `assume_a` for `scipy.linalg.solve`, they do have some standalone functions for specific structures, so it would be possible to support at least some of the options for each backend. `solve` with `assume_a="pos"` for a symmetric positive definite matrix is used in `scipy.signal.firls`. This option is available in JAX, and could be available through a cholesky solve for other backends.


##### controlling lapack driver

Some functions like `scipy.linalg.lstsq` and `scipy.linalg.svd` have an option `lapack_driver` for controlling which specific LAPACK routine is used. `jax.scipy.linalg.svd` has the `lapack_driver` kwarg but it is ignored. It seems there is no `jax.scipy.linalg.lstsq`.`torch.linalg.svd` and `torch.linalg.lstsq`, actually do have a driver `kwarg` which lets you pick specific routines from cusolver. `jax.lax.linalg.svd` also lets you pick specific routines from cusolver. `lapack_driver` could actually be supported on `torch` and on JAX if we delegate to `jax.lax.linalg.svd`. In this case `lapack_driver` would be kind of a misnomer though. Explicit control of the lapack driver for `lstsq` is used in `scipy.signal.firls` as a performance optimization that does not impact correctness. This seems to be the only place outside of tests and benchmarks where it is used.


##### optional additional return values

Some functions have optional kwargs that allow returning additional values. Such as the `return_rank` kwarg of `scipy.linalg.pinv` and `scipy.linalg.pinvh`. `jax.scipy.linalg` has neither `pinv` nor `pinvh`. Array API support for `return_rank` seems like it will require separately computing the `rank` with `xp.linalg.matrix_rank` or maybe doing something like implementing `pinv` in terms of `svd` where we can read off the rank from the svd. I don't think `return_rank` is used in SciPy outside of tests.


#### Discussion

I'd be happy to hear what other maintainers think about whether these `scipy.linalg` functions listed above should be given array support and to what extent it makes sense to support additional features. I think it may at least make sense to support `pivot` for `scipy.linalg.qr`, `assume_a` for `solve`, `check_finite` for eager backends, possibly `lapack_driver` for `svd` and `lstsq`, though it might make more sense to call it driver. Supporting the things that make sense on a best effort basis seems reasonable though. Then again, I don't have a strong opinion on this matter, I'm just trying to summarize the state of things to help us make an informed decision.

title: ENH: `special.gauss_legendre`: improve accuracy of weights
